spillover_issues.author: wmoss
spillover_issues.body:
Marin's Pulumi IaC has no single organizing convention: `infra/pulumi` splits into one GCP stack and four separate CoreWeave cluster stacks, `infra/buckets` spans GCS, CoreWeave object storage, and Cloudflare R2 in one stack, and Cloudflare DNS records are declared inline in three unrelated deploy stacks (`infra/grafana`, `infra/loom`, the CoreWeave federation stack) plus `infra/buckets`. Where a new resource belongs isn't predictable from any rule.

Evaluate consolidating to one stack per provider — GCP, CoreWeave, Cloudflare — with GitHub unchanged, since it's already provider-scoped.

**Prior research**

Full writeup, phase-by-phase migration plan, and `--target` mechanics: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/28f800f1-835e-479a-924c-596a10924138

The target model:
- **gcp** — absorbs `infra/pulumi`'s `marin` stack (federation-egress static IPs, GCLB/IAP, the `marin`/`marin-dev` Iris controllers' own VM-based provisioning, the project-wide IAM registry), the GCS slice of `infra/buckets`, and `infra/cloudsql`.
- **coreweave** — the four existing cluster stacks (NodePools, RBAC, Kueue, Traefik/cert-manager) merged into one, plus the CoreWeave object-storage slice of `infra/buckets`.
- **cloudflare** (new) — every DNS record (the federation CNAME, and each deploy stack's own record) plus R2, each record built from a `StackReference` into its owning stack rather than declared inline.
- `infra/ducky` and `infra/xprof` deploy through `iac.iris.service.IrisService`, a `local.Command` that shells to the Iris CLI rather than a `pulumi_gcp` resource — they don't own any GCP-provider resources and stay independent regardless of this change.

Benefits found: a single GCP stack makes authoritative GCP resources (e.g. a fully-owned IAM binding) safe to adopt, since GCP enforces authority per role/field and one stack means exactly one process ever computes a given role's complete membership — today's non-authoritative `*IAMMember` grants exist partly to avoid needing that guarantee across stacks. `infra/permissions` was already retired into the `marin` stack's `iac.gcp.iam.GcpIam` (#7576), so the same consolidation pattern has worked once before at smaller scale.

`pulumi up --target <urn> --target-dependents` lets one already-decided change land safely across a consolidated stack's resources — canary a CoreWeave config change cluster by cluster, or force one Cloud Run image bump without touching a sibling service. It doesn't reduce Pulumi's state lock, which is always stack-wide regardless of target scope, and the full program still evaluates and declares every resource on every run (a resource that's live but undeclared this run reads as "delete it," so a program can't skip building part of the graph to go faster).

That lock scope is why folding the GCP-hosted service deploys (Grafana, Echo, Evaldash, Loom) into the `gcp` stack is a separate, harder call than the rest of this. `.github/workflows/ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml` already auto-deploys Grafana, Echo, Evaldash, Ducky, and Xprof on every push to `main`, each against its own stack in its own `concurrency` group, so unrelated services deploy in parallel today with zero contention. Merging Grafana/Echo/Evaldash into one `gcp` stack means their independent, path-filtered, automated merges start queuing behind whichever one landed first, even when the two PRs touch disjoint resources — `--target` doesn't fix this, since the lock isn't scoped by target. Recovering today's parallelism would need `ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml` and `scripts/ci/pulumi_rollouts.py` rebuilt to resolve per-service URN target sets and either accept serialized deploys or build an explicit queue.

Given that cost, this consolidation is staged: land the GCP substrate, CoreWeave, and Cloudflare consolidation first (no CI-automation conflict, since none of that is part of the automated rollout pipeline); leave folding the Cloud Run/VM deploys into `gcp` as an explicit follow-up decision rather than a default consequence of adopting the convention.

Open question — fold Grafana/Echo/Evaldash/Loom into the `gcp` stack:
- For: one audit surface for the account's entire Cloud Run/VM/IAM footprint; one credential story.
- Against: trades five parallel, low-friction automated deploys for one shared lock; requires new CI automation (per-service target-set resolution, a queue or accepted serialization) before it's safe; reverses `infra/pulumi.md`'s stated reason Grafana got its own project — its own image and deployment lifecycle.

Done when: a decision is made on the GCP/CoreWeave/Cloudflare consolidation and, separately, on whether to pursue folding the GCP-hosted service deploys in. If the first is accepted, file follow-up issues for each stack's migration.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — design decision, no PR.** Definition of done here is "a decision is made" on a fleet-wide IaC convention; that's a human architecture call, not an agent-implementable change. I verified the issue's structural claims against the tree and found one thing worse than stated. Below is decision-ready grounding.

# Research

The claims hold. Current layout, verified:

- **1 GCP + 4 CoreWeave stacks** share `infra/pulumi` (project `marin-iac`): [`Pulumi.marin.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/Pulumi.marin.yaml) plus `Pulumi.cw-rno2a.yaml`, `Pulumi.cw-us-east-02a.yaml`, `Pulumi.cw-us-east-08a.yaml`, `Pulumi.cw-us-west-04a.yaml`.
- **`infra/buckets` is one cross-provider stack** — GCS + CoreWeave S3 + Cloudflare R2 providers all instantiated in [`buckets/__main__.py#L23-L39`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/buckets/__main__.py#L23-L39).
- **DNS is scattered across 6 sites, not 4** (correction to the issue): `infra/grafana` ([`__main__.py#L190`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/__main__.py#L190)), **`infra/echo` ([`__main__.py#L257`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/echo/__main__.py#L257))**, **`infra/evaldash` ([`__main__.py#L121`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/evaldash/__main__.py#L121))**, `infra/loom` ([`infrastructure.py#L620`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/loom/infrastructure.py#L620)), the CoreWeave federation CNAME ([`iac/coreweave/dns.py#L37`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/coreweave/dns.py#L37)), and R2 in `infra/buckets`. The issue named only grafana/loom/federation/buckets; echo and evaldash also declare `cloudflare.DnsRecord` inline. Cloudflare is the most fragmented provider — strengthens the consolidation case.
- **`ducky`/`xprof` own no GCP-provider resources** — both build `iac.iris.service.IrisService`, a `command.local.Command` shelling to the Iris CLI ([`iac/iris/service.py#L25-L26`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/iris/service.py#L25-L26)). Correctly excluded from the `gcp` target.
- **Parallel-deploy cost is real.** [`ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml) matrix-deploys ducky/echo/evaldash/grafana/xprof on push to `main`, each in `concurrency: group: pulumi-rollout-${{ matrix.name }}` (L88-90), driven by [`scripts/ci/pulumi_rollouts.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/ci/pulumi_rollouts.py). Folding these into one `gcp` stack serializes them behind one stack lock.
- **Precedent works.** `infra/permissions` is retired into `iac.gcp.iam.GcpIam` (#7576); [`permissions/__main__.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/permissions/__main__.py) now raises rather than deploying.

# Recommendation

Adopt the staged split the issue proposes; it is sound and the risky part is correctly isolated.

**Do now (low-risk, no CI-automation conflict):** consolidate to `gcp` (substrate) + `coreweave` (4 clusters merged) + new `cloudflare` (all 6 DNS sites + R2, each built from a `StackReference` into its owning stack). None of these are in the automated rollout pipeline, so no lock contention is introduced. File one follow-up migration issue per stack.

**Defer (needs a separate decision + CI rework):** folding the Cloud Run/VM service deploys (grafana/echo/evaldash/loom) into `gcp`. As the issue notes, `--target` does not scope the state lock, so this trades 5 parallel path-filtered auto-deploys for one serialized lock and requires rebuilding `ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml` + `pulumi_rollouts.py` to resolve per-service URN target sets first. Recommend **not** doing this now — the audit-surface/credential-story benefit doesn't outweigh reversing the documented reason ([`pulumi.md#L39-L49`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi.md#L39-L49)) each service got its own lifecycle.

**Coordinate with in-flight work first** — these touch the same GCP-stack IAM surface and should land before the `gcp` consolidation to avoid rebasing churn: #8455/#8458 (authoritative + centralized app IAM grants), #8459/#8462 (remove retired permissions stack). The authoritative-IAM goal in #8455 is in fact the strongest single argument *for* one `gcp` stack (one process computes each role's full membership), so sequence it deliberately.

Needs a maintainer decision on the two questions above before migration issues are filed. Handing off — no code change to make here.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
Setting `remat_mode="save_moe"` on the d1024 EP64 ladder rung (issue #8062 shape, `fixed_all_to_all` backend, capacity factor 1.8, histogram QB) corrupts training. Everything else held fixed against the rung baseline, the one-line change produced:

- train loss 2.798 at step 999 vs 2.216 for the baseline (+0.58 nats), diverged from early in the run
- `moe/drop_fraction` 4.5–8% for the whole run vs 1.75–1.79% reproduced across nine baseline draws at the same capacity factor
- median step 0.6125 s vs 0.6291 s (+2.7% throughput), consistent with the mode doing what it promises — skipping the re-execution of the six per-layer EP all-to-alls in backward recompute

Runs: [save_moe](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ar8062-13-518aec6b83) vs [baseline](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ar8062-10-0818d7c32).

A remat policy should be numerically neutral, and the baseline's drop trajectory is stable across placements and days, so this is not run-to-run variance: gradients under `save_only_these_names(*MOE_REMAT_SAVE_NAMES)` are wrong on this path. Likely suspects are the interaction of the named-save policy with the `custom_vjp` gather/scatter pair and `tree_checkpoint_name` tags in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_fixed_all_to_all.py` under the homogeneous layer scan, or the known all-to-all buffer-corruption class (ops wiki: "Ragged all-to-all can corrupt data").

Exposure today is limited: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep` hardcodes `recompute_all`, so hero and rung production runs are unaffected. But `experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py` exposes the mode via `SCALE_REMAT=save_moe`, where anyone reaching for the memory/speed trade would silently get corrupted training with finite loss — the failure does not crash.

Done when the root cause is identified and the mode is either fixed or removed for the EP backend. If fixed, it is worth re-measuring: +2.7% at the rung, and a host-offload variant of the same policy could make the trade viable at the d6144 hero, where saving the dispatch tensors on-device cannot fit.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
`materialize_ghalogs_step` hashes the absolute output path of its download step, so every step in the GHALogs chain gets a different hash per region and byte-identical data lands at a different path in each one.

`ghalogs_public_normalize_steps` passes `source_path=download.output_path` (`lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/diagnostic_logs.py:1456`), and `materialize_ghalogs_step` puts that value straight into `hash_attrs` as `"source_path"` (`:1400`). `download.output_path` resolves through `marin_prefix()`, so it carries the region bucket. The re-key propagates through the train partition, normalize, and everything keyed off normalize.

Reproduce:

```
for P in s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin gs://marin-us-central1 gs://marin-eu-west4; do
  MARIN_PREFIX=$P uv run python -c \
    "from marin.datakit.sources import all_sources; print(all_sources()['ghalogs/public'].normalized.name_with_hash)"
done
```

```
normalized/ghalogs/public_b268f659
normalized/ghalogs/public_80268c17
normalized/ghalogs/public_38a4a0b6
```

Every other registered source returns the same hash under all three. Downstream, that is four differing paths per region for this source: normalize, minhash, and tokenize under each of the two tokenizers.

Impact is that a region cannot reuse another region's GHALogs outputs, and any checked-in path record is only valid for the region it was generated in. `experiments/datakit/hero_data_paths.json` hit this: generated under a non-CoreWeave prefix, its four `ghalogs/public` entries pointed at paths that exist in no region. It is now pinned to `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin` to work around this.

`test_no_region_path_in_hash_attrs_except_known_bloom_gap` in `tests/datakit/test_reference_pipeline_hashing.py` asserts exactly this property but does not catch it, because it builds synthetic sources rather than the registry chains.

Expected: the GHALogs chain hashes an identity that does not vary by region, the way `quality_model_version` and `centroids_version` stand in for their region-specific paths elsewhere in the pipeline.

Note that any fix moves the output path for a source whose data is already materialized, so it needs a decision on whether to re-run or to map the existing outputs across.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
Accelerator-free Iris workloads are admitted with `kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-unconstrained-topology: "true"`, so Kueue places them with no domain preference. On `cw-us-east-08a` a single CPU-only job has spread across most of the cluster's NVLink domains and consumed several outright, stranding a large block of GB200 GPUs that are physically idle but unreachable by any gang.

This is a placement/packing gap, not the preemption gap fixed by #7928 — see "Relationship to #7916" below. It needs no upstream Kueue change.

## Observation

`cw-us-east-08a` at 2026-08-13T21:01Z. A substantial fraction of the fleet's GPUs are idle, several hundred GPU pods are pending — all `SchedulingGated` — and the large majority of the idle GPUs are unreachable.

`rav.datakit-fuzzy-validation-current-focus-prod-v16.zephyr-veri` holds a large set of GB200 nodes with per-pod requests of roughly **80% of a node's allocatable CPU, 90% of its memory, and zero GPUs**. Each occupied node therefore retains only a small CPU/memory remainder. The pending training pods request slightly more than that remainder on both axes, so they fit on neither. All 4 GPUs on each occupied node sit idle with no path to allocation.

Kueue reports it on the one workload that carries a condition (fleet counts elided):

```
couldn't assign flavors to pod set <id>: topology "multinode-nvlink-ib"
allows to fit only 2 out of 16 pod(s). Total nodes: <N>; excluded: resource "cpu": <nearly all>
```

Nodes are excluded on **cpu**, never on gpu.

## The packing problem

Placement is domain-blind, so the CPU job has landed roughly one pod per node spread across most NVLink domains rather than packing into a few. The resulting distribution is bimodal and close to worst-case for gang admissibility:

- **several domains consumed entirely** — no gang can use them
- **several more holed by only one or two pods each** — also unusable, because one such pod is enough to disqualify a node, and a gang needs a full domain

Which domain a CPU-only pod occupies is irrelevant to that pod, but decisive for gangs: a 16-replica GB200 gang binds hard to `nvlink.domain` (#7753), so it needs a whole domain's worth of free nodes. Cluster-wide, only a handful of nodes currently retain enough free CPU to host a gang pod at all, and they do not add up to a domain.

Packing the same pods into the minimum number of domains would leave the remainder untouched and admit several of the waiting gangs. The single-pod holes matter as much as the fully consumed domains.

## Relationship to #7916 / #7928

Same symptom, different mechanism — #7928 does not cover this case:

- In #7916 the blocking CPU work was priority-**0** batch, *below* the stalled interactive gangs. Preemption should have fired and was blocked by Kueue's non-TAS snapshot gap ([kubernetes-sigs/kueue#9992](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9992), still open).
- Here the CPU job is `iris-cpu-production` (**1000**) and the stalled gangs are `iris-coscheduled-batch` (**2**). Preemption is correctly never attempted; the CPU job outranks them legitimately.

So no preemption fix — local or upstream — resolves this. The capacity is lost at placement time, before priority is ever consulted. That also makes packing the only avenue that does not depend on kueue#9992 landing.

## Proposed direction

[`tasks.py#L950-L952`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L950-L952) currently stamps accelerator-free pods unconstrained:

```python
else:
    # Accelerator-free Pods remain in TAS without requesting colocation. This
    # records their per-node CPU usage in the same flavor as GPU gangs, so a
    # higher-priority gang can simulate reclaiming it before topology fit.
    metadata["annotations"][_KUEUE_UNCONSTRAINED_TOPOLOGY] = "true"
```

Unconstrained was the right call for #7928's goal (accounting CPU usage in the same flavor). It is under-specified for placement: "no colocation requirement" is being read as "no preference", and the resulting spread is what strands the GPUs.

Replacing the annotation with a **preferred** topology at the domain level would let Kueue pack accelerator-free pods into already-occupied domains and keep whole domains free, without making placement mandatory — a CPU pod must still be placeable anywhere when no packed domain has room. Preferred (not required) matters: these pods must never pend for topology reasons.

Worth confirming before implementing: that a preferred annotation on an otherwise unconstrained podset actually biases Kueue v0.18 toward already-occupied domains rather than merely tie-breaking, and that it does not regress the reclaim-simulation behavior #7928 added. If Kueue's preferred-level scoring does not pack, the fallback is a node-affinity preference computed by Iris at submit time.

## Reproduction

1. On `cw-us-east-08a`, submit accelerator-free tasks whose per-pod CPU request leaves less headroom than a gang pod needs, one per node, more than one domain's worth.
2. Group their assigned nodes by `ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain`.
3. Observe the pods spread across domains rather than packing.
4. Submit a 16-replica `GB200x4` gang and observe `SchedulingGated` with `excluded: resource "cpu"` while GPUs sit idle.

## Empirical check

Two 16-replica GB200x4 probe gangs, differing only in host-resource ask:

| probe | per-pod | result |
|---|---|---|
| `probe-gang16-lowcpu` | 4 GPU + small CPU/memory | admitted, all 16 tasks running within seconds |
| `probe-gang16-hicpu` | 4 GPU + production-sized CPU/memory | `SchedulingGated`, identical to the production gangs |

The GPUs are allocatable; host CPU/memory on the occupied nodes is the sole blocker. Both probes were stopped after the measurement.

## Notes

- Nearly all pending workloads carry **no status conditions at all**, some for well over an hour; only the queue head records the topology message. Whatever the cause, the queue gives operators no signal — the same "waited without their own admission condition" observation recorded in #7916. Placement auditing in #7481 is adjacent.
- The `cd-gp-i64-erapids` CPU pool cannot absorb this job — its nodes have well under half the cores one of these pods requests. See my comment on #7857: pinning CPU-only pods to that pool would make this workload unschedulable.

Add a verify step after each normalize step in the Datakit pipeline. The gate must stop downstream work when normalized shards violate ID properties.

- The verify step confirms that each shard has no duplicate `id` values.
- The verify step confirms that each shard is sorted by `id`.
- A failed check stops downstream steps and identifies the source and shard.
- Tests cover duplicate IDs, unsorted IDs, and valid normalized shards.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Feasibility input: MoK workspace cost on the doubled-expert configuration

Partial answer to the memory half of this issue, derived from the `mok_like` arena model rather than a run. It does not settle the throughput comparison, which still needs the matched gate this issue asks for.

### The workspace is independent of expert count, and linear in top-k

MoK's peer-visible workspace is sized by `(tokens_per_rank, hidden_dim, top_k, ranks)`. Expert count does not appear: `combine` and `d_x_routed` are `tokens x top_k x hidden`, and only the sync-flag arrays scale with rank count (about 1 KiB across the whole arena).

Two consequences for the doubled-expert candidate:

- **Going 192 -> 384 experts costs MoK nothing** in workspace.
- **Going top-4 -> top-8 doubles the two largest buffers.**

At the hero geometry (65,536 routed tokens/GPU, d6144):

| configuration | arena, 1 slot | 2 slots |
|---|---:|---:|
| current hero, top-4 | 7.50 GiB | 15.00 GiB |
| doubled-expert, top-8 | 13.50 GiB | 27.01 GiB |

So MoK's workspace grows by **+6.00 GiB per GPU per slot**, or +12.01 GiB at the two-slot configuration, purely from the routing change. Rank count is irrelevant: the same 7.50 GiB holds at EP4 and EP64.

### Why this matters here

#7279's doubled-expert attempts today were already memory-bound on the incumbent backend: MHEP-022 failed before step 0 at a 197.59 GiB estimate against a 171.64 GiB device limit, MHEP-023 failed the one-rack memory gate, and MHEP-024 only cleared its first step after trimming to 185.74 GiB. Adding a MoK workspace on top of a configuration with that little headroom is the central feasibility risk, and it is worth sizing before spending a rack on the matched comparison.

Two caveats that keep this from being a verdict:

1. **+12 GiB is an upper bound on the delta, not a net figure.** MoK replaces some existing dispatch and combine buffers, so the net change is smaller by whatever the incumbent path currently holds for the same purpose. Establishing the net requires the matched run.
2. **Single-slot operation halves it** to +6.00 GiB, at the cost of the two-slot overlap the sealed v15 configuration relies on. That is a real knob if memory is the binding constraint.

### Shape compatibility: no blockers found

- `mok_like` requires hidden and intermediate dimensions divisible by 256. The doubled-expert shape passes: 6144 % 256 = 0, expert width 3072 % 256 = 0. (Worth noting because the *earlier* i6272 hero shape would have failed this; #8132's move to hidden-wide 6144 incidentally made the shape MoK-compatible.)
- MoK requires shared experts, and the hero carries them, so the "shared expert absent from the hero" objection recorded on #8077 does not apply to the hero model itself.

### What is still required

The throughput and drop-rate halves of this issue are untouched. They need the matched gate against the selected non-MoK backend at the same model, routing, batch, runtime and hardware. That is blocked upstream on MoK reaching EP64 at all -- see #8244, where the fabric-handle transport is implemented but currently blocked in Iris gang bootstrap before any MoK code executes.

already provides that lifecycle, plus the `check_alive` and `backend_state` liveness
handling the TEI pool lacks: the pool yields once `min_ready_instances` of
`instances` register and never checks the pool again, so a run where most instances
crash-loop looks healthy and only moves slower. Reuse would also drop the pinned TEI
image, the apt/uv bootstrap in `_setup_script`, and the tar staging path.

Two known obstacles: `IrisServiceConfig` is bound to vLLM and Levanter engines, and
per #7998 the Marin stack would need a custom image or a reimplementation of the
embedding optimizations that TEI provides.

Done when: the Harrier pool runs through `marin/inference` with per-instance liveness
checks, or this issue records a measured throughput comparison that justifies keeping
TEI.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
PGLE cannot profile on the cw-us-east-08a GB200 racks, and with it enabled the EP hero's process-per-node gangs die two ways. Every run logs `PGLE collected an empty trace ... contention with another tool that subscribes to CUPTI` on every host (the node-level subscriber is unidentified; DCGM is the suspect — see the #8054 sweep record). Beyond being inert, the machinery is destructive on per-node gangs: auto-PGLE's trace sessions collide across compiled executables and abort the gang at dispatch (`ALREADY_EXISTS: Another profiling session active`, raised from `jax/_src/profiler.py:521` — captured with tracebacks in the [instrumented rerun](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5273968805)), and a run that survives dispatch can wedge silently at the FDO-recompile clique re-initialization (10.5 h stall at step 30, [forensics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5269927243)). The same gang completes cleanly with `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=false`.

Current mitigation: #8209 runs the EP hero one process per GPU, which cannot host PGLE at all (per-process CUPTI sessions collide) and defaults it off. That forgoes PGLE's measured upside — +1.1 MFU on a 1-rack d6144 lineage when it engaged (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5076593050) — which #6697 tracks capturing.

Done when: the node-level CUPTI subscriber is identified and deconflicted (or an upstream JAX/XLA fix for the profiling-session collision lands), a hero-shape run produces a verified non-empty PGLE trace, and an A/B against the PGLE-off baseline decides whether re-enabling pays.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Fuzzy verification in PR #8114 filters a broad set of duplicate candidates after connected-component clustering. This experiment measures whether removed documents are duplicates, whether retained candidates are missed duplicates or distinct documents, and whether the containment and unique-trigram limits should change. A small canary suggests that the current rules are precise but conservative. The 4K smoke and full-text review are in progress.

## Description

The audit reads full text from the CoreWeave source data and writes private reports to GCS. It samples removed, retained, boundary, random, source, length, score, and cluster-size strata. Corpus text stays in private artifacts.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Review at least 500 complete document comparisons, measure the quality of current decisions, test counterfactual parameter settings, and recommend either the current verifier or a measured parameter change. Run matched and larger samples after the 4K output passes its integrity checks.

## Status

The current 4K smoke contains 2,783 candidate clusters and 5,628 documents from 3,998 source shards. It uses 128 shuffle partitions and 32 workers. At 2026-08-11 18:44 UTC, stage 0 was complete and the verification stage was at 2/128 tasks. All 32 workers were alive after 14 preemptions, with no application error.

The exploratory canary has 47 reviewed candidate decisions:

- The current rules removed 4 candidates. All 4 appeared safe to remove.
- The rules retained 43 candidates. Manual review marked 28 as safe removal opportunities and 15 as unsafe to remove.
- The current rules found 4 of the 32 reviewed safe removal opportunities.
- A counterfactual containment limit of 0.90 with 8 unique trigrams found 7 safe removals and no unsafe removal. Limits of 0.85/8 and 0.80/8 found more safe removals but also 1 and 2 unsafe removals, respectively.

The canary is small and selected for inspection, so it does not support a production parameter change by itself. The production defaults have not changed.

A separate stress set contains 1,018 hard pairs from issue #6854. The current rule accepted three pairs, and all three were safe removals. A much smaller relaxation to 0.99 containment with 2 unique trigrams added 20 removals; directional review marked 16 safe and 4 unsafe because they lost a schedule month, a quote ending, an attribution, or a signature. This stress result is evidence against a global threshold reduction, including the canary-fitted 0.90/8 setting.

## Links

* Logbook: will be linked when the research branch is published
* W&B Report: none
* Important updates:
  * [PR #8114](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8114)
  * [4K V6 smoke](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Ffuzzy-verification-audit-4k-v6-20260811)

## Decision Log

- 2026-08-11: Bound the smoke shuffle at 128 partitions after an unbounded run created 3,998 downstream verification tasks.
- 2026-08-11: Set the smoke store-ready and recovery limits to 7,200 seconds after a 1,800-second deadline expired during worker recovery. This did not change production defaults.
- 2026-08-11: Defer parameter changes until the 4K integrity checks, stratified review, matched treatment, and larger samples are complete.

## Conclusion

Open. The final report requires at least three days of analysis and at least 500 complete document comparisons.

🤖 PR reconciliation found four items to resolve before merge:

- The multiple-canonical invariant has a missed path. Two same-ID, same-text records with two canonical flags are accepted because the representative-ID branch increments `canonicals_seen` and skips the `> 1` check. The current producer's source-prefixed CC IDs should prevent this state in a valid artifact, so this is a failed defensive invariant rather than an observed data error. Add the check and a same-ID regression test.
- The PR body says that each cluster uses its longest document, reaches the exhaustive ceiling, and needs no duplicate subgroups. The implementation selects the longest document only from the first 64 records or 2 million characters. Large-cluster replay found a safe duplicate subgroup that the current primary anchor missed. Narrow these claims to the measured sample.
- Update stale descriptions in `experiments/datakit/README.md`, `fuzzy_dups.py`, and the verifier test comment. Add a behavior test with more than 64 cluster records.
- Make the 64-record and 2-million-character anchor bounds explicit persisted configuration. They affect decisions but are absent from `VerifiedFuzzyDupsAttrData` and the verification step's `hash_attrs`.

The exact anchor-scan replay shows why a larger bound is not a direct fix. On clusters of size 22, 138, and 279, the current 64-record scan accepts 0 documents in 762 comparisons. A 32-record scan accepts 1 safe base-to-question-answer match in 761 comparisons. Scans of 128, 256, and the full cluster accept 0 in 764 comparisons because they select another anchor. Anchor recall is non-monotonic. A separate 128-local-representative replay finds one further safe capitalization-only duplicate that the current 64-representative limit misses.

The comparison-cap sweep does support the current value of 2 on the measured 4K, hashed, and large-cluster inputs:

- cap 1: 1,429 accepted, 3,911 comparisons
- cap 2: 1,432 accepted, 4,473 comparisons
- cap 4: 1,432 accepted, 5,044 comparisons
- cap 8: 1,432 accepted, 5,472 comparisons

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla
spillover_issues.body:
Reference implementation: https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens

## TL;DR — 2026-08-13

The supported `mok_like` path is ready for review and production extraction at the tested configuration. Confidence is high for numerical correctness, optimizer-state evolution, strict zero-drop routing, normal execution through two racks, and bounded propagation of synchronous native-handler failures. The final 32-process/128-GB200 run completed 100 updates with exact runtime audits and 83.77% weak-scale efficiency.

- Stable branch: [`codex/upstream-mok-like`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/upstream-mok-like)
- Snapshot tag: [`mok-like-v15-two-rack-2026-08-12`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/mok-like-v15-two-rack-2026-08-12)
- Commit: [`bceba3c7814f45f556109f202386f85c12844527`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/bceba3c7814f45f556109f202386f85c12844527)
- Final two-rack run: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mok-scale-012-v15-dropless-2rack-host176-100-20260812-1632) · [XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fmok-scale-012-v15-dropless-2rack-host176-100-20260812-1632)
- Detailed record: [barrier-free/zero-copy/scale logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/mok-like-v15-two-rack-2026-08-12/.agents/logbooks/8108-mok-like-barrier-free.md) · [earlier implementation logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/mok-like-v15-two-rack-2026-08-12/.agents/logbooks/8108-mixture-of-kittens-consolidation.md)
- Failure incident: [Echo wiki 137](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/137)

One combined property is unproven: cancellation while a healthy sibling invocation is simultaneously resident in the other workspace slot. Healthy two-slot overlap and one-failure/one-success isolation pass separately. Asynchronous CUDA context corruption remains process-terminal by design.

## Supported configuration

The sealed path uses:

- L48, width 6,144, E8/top-4, intermediate width 3,072, BF16 compute;
- one JAX process per four local GB200s, process-local EP4, and data parallelism across processes;
- strict schedule capacity factor 4, with zero dropped assignments in every sealed run;
- XLA-owned peer-visible forward inputs and staged backward peer storage;
- one native workspace slot;
- shared eager `cuda_async`, device-memory fraction 0.80, and no manual pool trims;
- a 176 GiB process-global pinned-host arena under a 900 GiB pod-memory request;
- local-only XLA per-fusion autotune cache;
- zero child retries, preemption retries, or tolerated task failures.

The launcher preset is still named `promoted_dropless_v12`; the native FFI schema in the tagged source is v15. Use the tag or commit, not the preset name, as native-version provenance.

## Confidence

| Area | Confidence | Evidence | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Healthy numerical training | High | Full forward/VJP comparisons, route extremes, dependent calls, concurrent calls, and 64 sequential momentum updates against an independent reference | Tested model shape, BF16 path, and optimizer sequence; not every possible model shape or dtype |
| Strict dropless routing | High | Capacity-factor-4 runs completed with exact zero dropped assignments on 4, 8, 64, and 128 GB200s | The guarantee depends on the supported factor-4 schedule and four-way local expert parallelism |
| Runtime protocol and slot reuse | High | Exact forward/backward handler counts, generation checks, slot audits, and zero protocol anomalies through 100 updates on 32 processes | Normal path uses one slot; two-slot reuse is covered by targeted correctness gates rather than the final training run |
| Synchronous failure closure | High within scope | Four isolated forward/backward failure points closed in under one second on four GB200s; a process-zero backward failure became the same error on both JAX processes in about 3.23 seconds and both tasks exited cleanly | Requires a usable independent cancellation stream; asynchronous sticky CUDA failures are terminal |
| Failure isolation with concurrent RunIds | Medium-high | One injected failure and one numerically correct success completed without generation or reuse anomalies | The short failure gates serialized before slot overlap; simultaneous failed/healthy residency is not proven |
| One-rack and two-rack execution | High for the tested shape | 16-process/64-GB200 and 32-process/128-GB200 gates completed with finite losses, zero drops, exact all-process audits, and clean Iris exits | Does not prove different expert group sizes, more than two racks, or much longer training horizons |
| Throughput | Medium-high | Matched two-node v15/v12 pair, one-rack v15/v12 pair, and a 100-step two-rack v15 seal | Two-rack v12 runs showed fabric-related variance; one successful v15 long run does not eliminate cluster variance |
| Host-memory margin | High for 900 GiB pods | 176 GiB arena passed one node, one rack, and two racks; the final run retained 106.5 GiB cgroup headroom with zero memory events | Do not reduce the 900 GiB pod request without a separate full-rack cgroup gate |

## Final results

### Numerical and stateful parity

The 64-step stateful gate alternated balanced, zero-token, skewed, and all-to-one routes while applying sequential momentum updates. Outputs, losses, all gradients, parameters, and optimizer state stayed within the configured numerical tolerances. Drops and inactive-expert gradients were exactly zero. The run completed 256 forward and 256 backward handlers, used slot zero only, and reported zero generation or reuse anomalies.

The broader correctness matrix also covered balanced and adversarial routing, 1/2/8/32-macrobatch schedules, offloaded saved context, dependent back-to-back VJPs, concurrent executions, corrupt saved-context stamps, and strict all-to-one capacity.

### Failure closure

V15 returns a scalar failure status from native forward/backward calls. Generation- and slot-scoped device cancellation releases the local EP4 peer group. A `lax.pmax` over non-expert mesh axes makes the failure decision uniform before later shared-weight collectives. Those collectives execute only in the success branch; the failure branch raises through a pure typed-FFI fence.

This structure came from two failures in earlier candidates:

1. Device-only cancellation let healthy ranks leave the FFI and enter later `lax.psum` calls after another rank failed. The distributed job then hung.
2. Uniform failure propagation initially left backward registered as an ordered side effect. JAX retained the expected failure in its runtime token and raised it again during `effects_barrier()` at interpreter shutdown.

Making backward destination-passing and pure removed the retained ordered token. The negative distributed harness closes the native runtime and calls `jax.distributed.shutdown()` explicitly after checking the uniform error.

The accepted two-process gate injected a backward failure on process zero before input readiness. Both processes observed the same phase-neutral error in 3.2309 and 3.2367 seconds. Each reported four forward and four backward handlers, `[2, 0]` slot acquisitions on every local rank, maximum active slots one, and zero generation or reuse anomalies. Both Iris tasks exited zero.

### Performance and scale

| Run | Devices | Window | Total tok/s | Tok/s/GPU | Weak-scale efficiency | Result |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| V12 matched baseline | 8 | 60–79 | 38,632.67 | 4,829.08 | 93.48% against four-GPU dropless baseline | Pass |
| V15 matched candidate | 8 | 60–79 | 40,110.63 | 5,013.83 | 97.05% against the same baseline | Pass; +3.83% vs v12 pair |
| V12 host-176 one-rack | 64 | 10–24 | 314,110.12 | 4,907.97 | 95.00% | Pass |
| V15 host-176 one-rack | 64 | 10–24 | 309,026.65 | 4,828.54 | 93.47% | Pass; −1.62% vs v12 pair |
| V12 long two-rack | 128 | 60–79 | 516,415.19 | 4,034.49 | 78.10% | Correctness pass; performance gate miss |
| V15 long two-rack | 128 | 60–79 | 553,963.07 | 4,327.84 | 83.77% | Pass; +7.27% vs long v12 run |

The final v15 two-rack run used exactly two hard NVLink domains with 16 nodes each. All 32 tasks completed 100 finite zero-drop rows. Every process reported 19,200 forward and 19,200 backward handlers, zero forward staging, exactly 76,800 staged-backward calls and 30,964,029,849,600 staged bytes, slot one unused, maximum active slots one, and zero protocol, generation, reuse, trim, or slot anomalies.

The matched two-node pair showed no measurable scalar failure-agreement overhead; the v15 arm was faster in that pair. Process-zero HBM was 5.73 GiB higher in the v15 W&B sample than in the v12 baseline, but both runs completed without device-memory errors. The source of the sampled HBM difference is unresolved.

### Host memory

The original 192 GiB pinned-host arena left little margin under a 900 GiB pod. Direct cgroup and `smaps` measurements showed that the approximately 816 GiB peak was real process-private anonymous memory, not double-counted descendants.

- A 128 GiB arena failed before step zero when each host BFC allocator attempted a 99 GiB allocation.
- A 176 GiB arena passed 25 steps and reduced the one-node cgroup peak by 70.18 GiB relative to the 192 GiB control without a throughput regression.
- The v15 one-rack run peaked at 805.90 GiB, leaving 94.10 GiB of cgroup headroom.
- The final v15 two-rack run peaked at 793.49 GiB on process zero, leaving 106.51 GiB of cgroup headroom. All memory-event counters stayed zero.

The promoted arena is 176 GiB. The pod request remains 900 GiB.

## What was tried and rejected

### Communication and staging

- Global peer barriers worked but cost throughput. Generation-tagged producer readiness and destination completion replaced them.
- XLA one-shot symmetric copying was correct but roughly an order of magnitude too slow.
- Device-initiated ragged transfer improved the first implementation but remained slower than the fused path.
- Forward zero-copy improved the staged control by about 0.5% in the matched four-GB200 comparison and is promoted.
- Full backward zero-copy was numerically correct but 2.40% slower than staged backward. Hybrid variants recovered most of the loss but did not beat forward-only zero-copy. Staged backward is promoted.

### Capacity and routed-weight gradients

- Schedule factor 1.1 was fast but not dropless; the sealed 100-step control dropped about 0.15% of assignments in the scored window.
- The original capacity-dependent routed-weight-gradient result made strict factor-4 graphs too large.
- One canonical FP32 routed-weight-gradient result per local expert removed that capacity-dependent XLA reduction. Factor 4 then completed route extremes and full-model scale gates with exact zero drops.

### Device allocation

- Shared eager `cuda_async` at fraction 0.85 repeatedly failed on the same 132,687,700,848-byte temporary near update 66.
- Raising the fraction, using one workspace slot, synchronizing results, VMM, recurring manual trims, and parallel trim did not remove the deterministic failure.
- V12 telemetry showed that trim returned physical backing exactly, graph-pool memory was zero, and bytes outside the default pool stayed constant. The failure was tight default-pool large-allocation reuse, not a graph-memory or external-allocation leak.
- A separate temp pool and shared on-demand allocation completed but cost about 17% throughput.
- Shared eager allocation at fraction 0.80 crossed update 66 and completed 100 steps without trims. This is the promoted setting.

### Failure-control tests

- Blocking a host callback until a second invocation leased a slot caused a five-minute circular wait because PJRT could not dispatch the second callback on that occupied lane.
- A nonblocking lease-count hook could miss the injection when both callbacks observed insufficient overlap.
- Injecting on the second distinct invocation key produced one expected failure and one correct success, but the short calls serialized through slot zero. Compiling separate static call sites also serialized.
- A correct combined overlap proof requires a test-only, generation-safe device witness. The witness must observe both invocations resident without blocking a host callback. It is not part of the stable implementation.

## Unproven and out of scope

1. Cancellation while a healthy sibling is concurrently resident in the other workspace slot is not proven in one gate. Healthy same-executable two-slot overlap and one-failure/one-success isolation are proven separately.
2. Asynchronous illegal-address faults or sticky CUDA context corruption do not have bounded in-process recovery. The process must terminate and be replaced by the job supervisor.
3. More than two racks, local expert groups larger than four GPUs, other model shapes, other dtypes, and runs longer than 100 optimizer updates have not been sealed.
4. Full backward zero-copy remains an optimization target. It is not the supported configuration because the measured path was slower.
5. Cross-rack throughput varies with the fabric. The final v15 run passed 80%, but an earlier v12 run reached only 78.10% with a wide step-time tail and no numerical or protocol failure.
6. The 5.73 GiB process-zero HBM difference in the matched v15/v12 pair is not attributed.
7. The branch is a reproducible research snapshot, not yet merged into the repository default branch.

## Decision log

- 2026-08-10: remove global peer barriers; use generation-tagged readiness and completion.
- 2026-08-11: promote forward zero-copy and staged backward; reject full backward zero-copy on throughput.
- 2026-08-11: use canonical FP32 routed-weight gradients and schedule factor 4 for strict zero-drop routing.
- 2026-08-11: use shared eager `cuda_async` at fraction 0.80; reject manual trim and on-demand/separate-pool paths.
- 2026-08-12: propagate synchronous failures as device data before later collectives; make backward pure destination-passing FFI.
- 2026-08-12: promote the 176 GiB pinned-host arena while retaining the 900 GiB pod request.
- 2026-08-12: advance v15 after matched two-node, one-rack, and two-rack gates passed.

## Handoff

The tagged v15 snapshot is the stable implementation for the supported configuration. The next repository change should extract it into a reviewable PR without changing the sealed runtime or launcher defaults. Review should focus on the failure-status dataflow, pure backward FFI contract, generated native wait/cancellation code, pinned-host preset, and exact all-process audit schema.

Do not block adoption on the combined failed/healthy overlap witness unless that property is a production requirement. If it is required, build the witness on a confidence branch and retain the strict acceptance condition: both workspace slots active, one expected failure, one numerically correct success, exact per-slot counters, and zero generation or reuse anomalies.

Keep the issue open until the stable snapshot is merged or an explicit decision is made to retain it as an experiment-only branch.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The reference builds one deterministic device schedule. One Blackwell kernel then runs dispatch, shared and routed FFNs, and combine.

It uses [NCCL symmetric buffers and remote TMA](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens/blob/6438bf48f88094d305972fbe0fa6deba0f7d4d1a/csrc/mok_megakernel.cuh), [pull-based scheduling with 256-row expert padding](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens/blob/6438bf48f88094d305972fbe0fa6deba0f7d4d1a/csrc/scheduler.cuh), and separate communication and compute SMs. Marin has [JAX ragged all-to-all](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a5f0269edc35a3766958adb494cef7d371632ebd/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L28-L124) and [Blackwell grouped GEMMs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a5f0269edc35a3766958adb494cef7d371632ebd/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/quack_moe_cute.py#L75-L174). JAX 0.11 also includes XLA flags for NCCL symmetric buffers and one-sided ragged all-to-all.

Issue #7973 lists the forward port as an agent evaluation task. This issue will own the Marin implementation, benchmark results, and reproducible artifacts.

# Proposed Fix

## Design

I will implement three measured increments under the `MOK-JAX` experiment prefix.

1. `MOK-JAX-001` will implement the deterministic schedule in JAX. It will match peer interleaving, 256-row expert padding, and padding sentinel values.
2. `MOK-JAX-002` will add a BF16 forward experiment. It will compare XLA private and symmetric ragged all-to-all with the same routing and grouped-GEMM work.
3. `MOK-JAX-003` will prototype one fused collective FFI kernel only if the first two increments identify a useful target.

XLA symmetric memory is part of the second increment. The flag registers eligible collective buffers. The symmetric ragged all-to-all mode selects XLA's one-sided Put and Signal path.

The flag does not fuse transport with the expert MLP. XLA supports symmetric buffers for collective FFI calls, but those C++ context headers are not in jaxlib's public include package.

## Success criteria

- Schedule outputs match an independent host reference for balanced, skewed, and padded routes.
- BF16 output and gradients match the existing Marin EP reference at Marin test tolerances.
- The uncapped correctness configuration drops no assignments.
- Private and symmetric modes have per-stage Finelog measurements on GB200.
- A fused kernel starts only if the profile assigns enough time to removable kernel boundaries or host coordination.

## Costs and risks

The symmetric path is experimental and tied to JAX 0.11, NCCL, and the XLA collective allocator. The full fused kernel is Blackwell-specific.

The external reference uses loose BF16 and MXFP8 test tolerances. Marin tests will use the repository numerical policy.

## Testing

I will add CPU schedule tests first. I will then run multi-device correctness and short performance screens before a larger benchmark.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: barrier-free runtime, zero-copy, dropless capacity, and allocator stabilization

David continued the experiment after the handoff above. This update covers the four-GB200 work completed in the current session and the remaining scale gates.

### Barrier-free supported path

- Consolidated the PyTorch-free native adapter under `levanter.kernels.mixture_of_kittens` and connected it to the normal Grug E8/top-4 model path.
- Replaced all four global peer barriers with generation-tagged producer readiness and destination completion. A later cleanup deleted the dead peer-barrier kernel, launcher, signal allocations, and legacy counter fields.
- Added explicit static `collective_id`, invocation-wide cancellation, one-shot slot release, slot-parity generations, saved-context stamps, quiescent ordinal reclamation, and mutually exclusive runtime maintenance.
- Balanced, zero-token, 3:1 skew, all-to-one, 1/2/8-macro, offloaded-context, dependent back-to-back VJP, and concurrent same-executable VJP gates pass. The corrupt-stamp gate traps immediately without hanging or reusing the slot.
- The 100-step staged barrier-free control completed with zero protocol anomalies: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mok-bf-010-zero-barrier-100-s80n5-r1-20260810-1900) · [XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fmok-bf-010-zero-barrier-100-s80n5-r1-20260810-1900). Steps 60–79 averaged 20,966.88 raw and 20,935.97 drop-adjusted tok/s, 12.5030 s, and 24.5217% MFU.

Confidence: stable on the tested four-GB200 workload. Native handler counts, generation mismatches, slot-reuse failures, and all-process protocol summaries are checked explicitly.

### XLA-owned peer-visible buffers and zero-copy

- A standalone typed-FFI ring probe proved exact remote reads and writes from XLA-owned buffers on four GB200s. Collective memory space 1 worked but inserted three optimized-HLO boundary copies. Default memory space 0 preserved zero optimized-HLO copies and also passed two concurrent executions with distinct `RunId`s. Equal virtual addresses are unnecessary because the runtime exchanges a per-peer pointer table.
- Production forward now publishes each rank's XLA `x` pointer through invocation-local state and skips the forward staging copy. The existing ready/completion protocol closes the remote-read lifetime before the FFI call returns.
- Forward zero-copy passed full forward/VJP parity, dependent-call reuse, and concurrent same-executable VJPs. The 100-step run completed at [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mok-zc-013-forward-only-100-s80n5-r1-20260810-2355) with [XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fmok-zc-013-forward-only-100-s80n5-r1-20260810-2355). Steps 60–79 averaged 21,074.51 raw and 21,023.83 adjusted tok/s, 12.4394 s, and 24.6476% MFU: +0.51% raw throughput versus staged.
- Direct backward peer inputs and direct router-gradient output are numerically correct, including concurrent VJPs and route extremes, but the all-direct 100-step arm averaged 20,463.28 tok/s over steps 60–79, 2.40% below staged. A hybrid that staged only the 1 MiB router-gradient output recovered staged parity but remained 0.36% below forward-only. Backward producer-readiness costs consumed the copy savings.

Decision: keep forward zero-copy and staged backward. Full backward zero-copy remains an optimization target, not the promoted setting.

### Dropless capacity and routed-weight gradients

- The original factor-1.1 schedule is not dropless. The barrier-free 100-step control dropped 0.148% of assignments over steps 60–79; strict all-to-one routing requires factor 4 on four ranks.
- Replaced one FP32 routed-weight-gradient result per static macrobatch with one canonical FP32 result per local expert. The native epilogue serializes the first store and later `store_add` contributions, removing the capacity-dependent XLA reduction. Correctness passes for 8-macro balanced routes, zero-token experts with exactly zero inactive gradients, and 32-macro all-to-one routes.
- Strict factor-four one-layer/two-update and 48-layer/two-update runs completed with zero drops. The 48-layer warm update reached 11,892.91 tok/s versus 12,337.68 tok/s for the factor-1.1 control, a preliminary 3.6% raw gap. The old capacity-dependent factor-four graph OOMed before step zero; the canonical-gradient graph completed.

Confidence: strict capacity is correct and executable for short full-model gates. A matched 100-step dropless throughput result is still missing.

### Allocator investigation

- Canonical routed gradients exposed a repeatable `cuda_async` failure on a 132,687,700,848-byte temporary. Raising the allocator fraction, full-result synchronization, VMM, one workspace slot, and manual pool trims did not produce a stable 100-step treatment. VMM could not fit the physical-allocation budget. Separate-temp and shared on-demand allocation completed but ran at about 17.45k tok/s, roughly 17% below staged.
- Native v12 telemetry measured physical free memory, default-pool used/reserved memory, and CUDA graph-pool memory at each quiescent trim. `cudaMemPoolTrimTo` returned 134,452,609,024 bytes per rank, and physical free memory rose by exactly that amount. Graph memory stayed zero. Bytes outside the default and graph pools were constant to the byte across 13 checkpoints. The update-66 failure is internal default-pool large-allocation reuse under a tight retained threshold, not a leak.
- Lowering eager preallocation/release threshold from fraction 0.85 to 0.80 retained the fast asynchronous pool and completed 55 steps without trims or allocator errors: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mok-dl-026-cap11-v12-eager80-55-20260811-0815) · [XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fmok-dl-026-cap11-v12-eager80-55-20260811-0815). Steps 45–54 averaged 20,984.08 raw tok/s, 12.4926 s, and 24.5418% MFU. All handler, staging, slot, and protocol audits passed.
- The 100-step seal is [active](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mok-dl-027-cap11-v12-eager80-100-20260811-0834). At the latest observed checkpoint it had completed 68 finite updates, crossed the prior deterministic update-66 failure boundary, and remained near 12.9 s/update without an allocator error.

Confidence: the 55-step allocator result is replicated through the prior early failure boundaries. Promotion still requires the active 100-step terminal audit and steps 60–79 profile.

### Scaling preparation

- Relaxed the single-process restriction only for process-local EP4 groups. A concrete-mesh preflight requires each expert slice to be exactly one process's four local devices; native pointer exchange never crosses a host.
- A two-node, one-layer, two-update smoke completed with one JAX process per four-GPU task. Each process recorded the expected eight forward/eight backward handlers and zero generation/reuse/protocol errors.
- Added an explicit local-only XLA per-fusion autotune-cache mode. It preserves the compilation cache but skips the remote stage-down that delayed single-node startup by 5–15 minutes. The first local-only run entered model/native setup in under one minute.
- Added all-process audit aggregation for handler counts, forward staging bytes, slot use, protocol errors, and allocator maintenance. Child failure, preemption, and cumulative task retries are all zero for the scale gates.

One-rack and two-rack measurements have not run. The next order is:

1. Finish the active factor-1.1 100-step seal.
2. Run the matched strict-dropless factor-four 100-step arm.
3. Create and validate a clean source snapshot; the current implementation is still an uncommitted research worktree.
4. Run 2-node, 16-node, then 32-node gates with process-local EP4 groups. The 32-node interactive request is expected to exceed the current `dlwh` budget and needs an authorized budget or production band.

EP64 now runs through the Marin/JAX MoK adapter on one GB200 NVLink domain. The accepted topology is 16 Iris tasks × 4 supervised one-GPU JAX processes, for 64 JAX processes and an expert mesh of `(replica=1, data=1, expert=64, model=1)`. The implementation is on [`codex/mok-ep64-probe`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/mok-ep64-probe) at [`1f19acefe1`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/1f19acefe19c52ff5c2497c8199f44eced811776).

The current confidence level is **medium for bounded capacity-limited EP64 execution, not production promotion**. The 64-GPU transport and two-update native path are high-confidence within the tested shape. A nine-update repetition stalled before its first optimizer row, and strict factor-64 capacity also stalled before its first row. Those two limits are unresolved.

### What is implemented

- One GPU per supervised JAX process, with 64 processes placed in one hard `ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain`.
- PyTorch 2.11 CUDA Symmetric Memory used only as the fabric-memory allocator/rendezvous layer. Marin retains JAX ownership of execution and the MoK native kernel.
- One 8,055,170,816-byte symmetric arena per rank. Each rank maps explicit pointers for all 64 peers; no symmetric virtual address assumption is required.
- A distinct native v16 EP64 ABI and `dispatch<64>` path. EP4 remains separate and unchanged.
- Runtime-staged forward and backward storage, one workspace slot, exact 64-bit peer masks, and regression coverage at ranks 31, 32, and 63.
- Exact per-peer generation/readiness/completion/cancellation cells, full-expert-axis failure agreement, collective initialization rollback, and failure-preserving teardown.
- Scanned reverse-backward validation accepts an older saved forward stamp after newer layer forwards while still rejecting a corrupt checksum.
- A one-rack launcher with E128/top-4, width 6,144, intermediate width 3,072, global batch 1,024, EP64/DP1, 176 GiB pinned-host limit, 900 GiB pod memory, and zero retries.

Local validation at the accepted commit: 162 focused/legacy tests passed; Ruff, Black, Pyrefly, AST, license, merge-conflict, whitespace, and large-file checks passed. Pinned MoK/ThunderKittens source generation passed with only 64-bit peer shifts.

### Passed hardware gates

**64-rank fabric transport.** A standalone one-rack probe completed on all 64 ranks with CUDA Symmetric Memory, one common fabric UUID/clique, 64 peer pointers and 64 signal pointers per rank, all-peer reads/writes, explicit rank 31/32/63 coverage, post-JAX device work, and clean 64-process teardown. This proves the GB200 workload pods expose working IMEX/fabric mappings across one NVLink domain.

**Two-layer/two-update native smoke.** [`mok-ep64-native-009-2l2s-20260813-2109`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mok-ep64-native-009-2l2s-20260813-2109) passed:

- 16/16 tasks and 64/64 supervised processes exited zero;
- finite losses `11.8091946 → 10.0266924`, with zero drops on both rows;
- every process reported exactly 4 forward and 4 backward handlers;
- exact staged bytes: 3,221,225,472 forward and 6,450,839,552 backward per process;
- slot-zero acquisitions 8 per process, slot one unused, maximum active slots one;
- generation mismatches, reuse failures, protocol errors, trim activity, and trim anomalies all zero.

**Full 48-layer/two-update hero shape.** [`mok-ep64-native-010-48l2s-20260813-2115`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mok-ep64-native-010-48l2s-20260813-2115) passed:

- one hard NVLink domain, 16×4 GB200, 64/64 native runtimes initialized, and all tasks/processes exited zero;
- finite losses `11.8072157 → 10.5438328`;
- every process reported exactly 96 forward and 96 backward handlers;
- exact staged totals per process: 96 forward calls / 77,309,411,328 bytes and 384 backward calls / 154,820,149,248 bytes;
- slot-zero acquisitions 192 per process, slot one unused, maximum active slots one;
- all generation, reuse, protocol, trim, and audit anomaly fields zero;
- sampled peak per task was 229.45 GiB host memory and 178,587/189,471 MiB HBM per GPU (94.26%).

The second row dropped 56,086,187 assignments, a 6.9646% drop fraction. This is expected under schedule factor 4 on EP64 and is why this mode is labeled capacity-limited, not dropless.

### What was tried and what failed

The transport bring-up exposed several non-runtime failures before the accepted probe: an outdated NVML XML parser, Gloo advertising loopback, an invalid hard-coded `eth0`, and an unnecessary `symm_mem.set_backend("CUDA")` call. PyTorch 2.11 already had CUDA active; removing that call and dynamically selecting the pod interface produced the EP8 pass. The first EP64 transport attempt then timed out on five source ranks because host/device phases were not aligned; bounded Gloo and CUDA synchronization around each probe phase fixed it, and the next 64-rank attempt passed.

Native attempts also found and fixed two bootstrap races:

- four supervised processes in each pod raced to clone the pinned source into one path; file locking plus atomic materialization fixed it;
- expensive source/build work happened before the first 64-rank rendezvous, so one compiler straggler left 63 ranks in a JAX broadcast; moving symmetric workspace alignment before native build fixed it.

One later rack attempt failed before code startup because all pods lost the route to the Iris controller while fetching the workspace bundle. The following coordinator was blocked by a temporary CoreWeave object-store write suspension. The accepted runs reused the same immutable Iris bundle and placed only smoke-step metadata on coordinator-local disk; model/data/native behavior was unchanged and W&B remained durable.

**Strict factor 64 is not working.** A two-layer/one-update factor-64 run mapped all arenas, initialized all 64 native runtimes, and entered the optimizer loop, but produced no row. All 64 runners became uniformly futex-idle, all GPUs stayed at 0% utilization, and host/HBM usage remained well below limits. It was stopped after a bounded observation window. This is a distributed dispatch/wait failure, not an OOM, and strict worst-case dropless EP64 must not be claimed.

**Nine-update stability is not sealed.** A full 48-layer factor-4 run mapped and initialized all 64 ranks and reached fused loss on every rank, then became uniformly futex-idle before step zero completed. W&B had zero rows; all GPUs were idle; sampled host memory was 247.55 GB against the 900 GiB request; no traceback, OOM, or native fatal appeared. It was stopped after the successful two-update run's timing envelope was exceeded. The dependence on `num_train_steps` points to compile/dispatch or optimizer-schedule graph behavior rather than proven native corruption, but root cause is unknown.

### Confidence and explicit non-claims

| Area | Confidence | Evidence | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64-GPU fabric mapping | High | All-peer EP64 probe passed on all ranks with explicit 31/32/63 coverage | Proven for one GB200 NVLink domain only |
| Native forward/backward correctness plumbing | Medium-high | Two-layer and 48-layer two-update runs completed with exact all-rank audits and finite loss | No independent EP64 numerical reference comparison yet |
| Scan/generation/slot protocol | High for serial one-slot execution | 6,144 forward + 6,144 backward handlers in the 48-layer run, exact counters, zero anomalies | Concurrent/re-entrant EP64 is forbidden; only one slot is supported |
| Capacity-limited factor 4 | Medium | Full 48-layer two-update pass | Drops are material; 6.96% observed on one row |
| Strict dropless factor 64 | Low / unsupported | Initialization passed, first update hung uniformly | No optimizer row; do not call EP64 dropless |
| Longer-run stability | Low | Nine-update gate hung before step zero | Only two optimizer updates are sealed |
| Failure closure | Low for EP64 | Failure plumbing is implemented and locally tested | No 64-rank injected-failure hardware gate yet |
| Performance | Unmeasured | Both passing jobs were compile/startup dominated | No profile-free throughput window or XProf seal |

Additional boundaries:

1. EP64 requires one workspace slot, staged forward/backward buffers, and identical synchronous SPMD call order across all 64 processes.
2. XLA-owned peer-pointer zero copy is not supported across processes.
3. Async illegal-address/sticky CUDA failures remain process-terminal.
4. The current schedule factor 4 is capacity-limited. Factor 64 is the strict all-to-one bound and currently hangs.
5. No 64-rank adversarial route-parity suite, injected-failure matrix, 25/100-step run, or profile-free throughput comparison has passed.
6. The shared object-store write incident required a local metadata path for the accepted smoke runs; normal artifact persistence should be rechecked after the storage service is healthy.

### Recommended next work

Do not promote EP64 as the default backend yet. Preserve `1f19acefe1` as the first functioning snapshot and investigate the pre-row all-rank wait with a synthetic fixed-batch harness that removes the data pipeline and W&B/artifact hooks. Compare lowered/compiled graphs for `num_train_steps=2` versus 9 and factor 4 versus 64, then add a bounded stage marker around schedule build, native FFI entry/return, failure `pmax`, and optimizer collectives. Once the first-step stall is resolved, require:

1. independent EP64 forward/VJP parity on balanced, zero-token, skewed, and all-to-one routes;
2. 64-rank injected failures before readiness and completion, with uniform errors and clean teardown;
3. at least 25 finite updates with exact all-rank audits;
4. a profile-free throughput window and XProf capture;
5. either a passing strict factor-64 gate or an explicit product decision to accept capacity-limited EP64 with measured drop/quality tradeoffs.

Durable local monitoring records:

- `scratch/20260813-1208_ep64_symm_mem_monitoring_state.json`
- `scratch/20260813-2109_ep64_native_009_monitoring_state.json`
- `scratch/20260813-2115_ep64_native_010_monitoring_state.json`
- `scratch/20260813-2140_ep64_native_011_monitoring_state.json`
- `scratch/20260813-2159_ep64_native_012_monitoring_state.json`
