comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-16 — Both hero width asymmetries now run in the fused kernel; 25.28% MFU dropless on one rack

### What changed

The megakernel derived one width for the routed and shared paths on two separate axes. Both are now split, so the hero shape runs unpinned:

- **Token width.** `ForwardBf16` takes `routed_x` beside `x`; `BackwardBf16` takes `routed_x` and `grad_routed_output` and returns `d_routed_x` beside `d_x`. The shared-plus-routed sum moved out of the FFI epilogue into JAX, so `mok_like_mlp` expands the routed combine through `w_latent_up` before adding the shared output. `latent_dim` is no longer rejected in `model.py`.
- **Intermediate width.** The routed experts carry their own intermediate dim, so the hero's 6144 routed against 3072 shared is expressible.

`globals_fwd.x_shared` is only ever a rank-local GEMM operand, so it now points at the XLA input directly and needs no staging or peer mapping. The symmetric arena therefore holds only routed tensors: 7.50 → 3.75 GiB per rank at the EP64 production shape.

The launcher stops pinning `latent_dim` and both intermediate dims. `--latent-dim`, `--routed-intermediate-dim`, `--shared-intermediate-dim`, `--batch-size-per-node`, `--mok-like-num-comm-sms`, and `--mok-like-minibatch-size/--mok-like-macrobatch-size` move both arms together.

### Result

One rack, 16 layers, hidden 6144, latent 3072, routed intermediate 6144, shared 3072, capacity factor 1.1, 128 sequences per node:

| | MFU | tokens/s | dropped assignments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| sample 1 | 25.28% | 853,302 | 0 |
| sample 2 | 25.42% | 857,839 | 0 |
| sample 3 | 25.14% | 848,445 | 0 |

Sixteen layers is a third of hero depth, so 853,000 tokens/s is about 284,000 normalised to forty-eight. MFU is the depth-normalised metric: at a fixed macrobatch depth does not move it, 23.85% at 16 layers against 23.83% at 48 on the pinned width.

Contributions, each measured matched at 16 layers on one node:

| change | MFU | dropped |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pinned routed intermediate 3072 | 23.85% | 0 |
| routed intermediate 6144 | 25.11% (mean of five: 25.35 / 25.10 / 24.63 / 25.34 / 25.13) | 0 |
| capacity factor 4.0 → 1.1, 48 layers | 23.13% → 23.83% | 0 |
| 64 → 128 sequences per node, one rack | 24.19% → 25.28% | 0 |

Capacity factor 1.1 costs nothing in drops because the drops are a router transient. Factor 1.0 is worse on both axes. Per-node batch matters because the data-parallel reduction costs the same per step whatever the batch; 128 sequences per node puts the rack's global batch at 2,048, which the sealed two-rack runs already used.

Negative results: the comm-SM split, minibatch and macrobatch sizes, `save_moe`, and a higher device-memory fraction each lost to the defaults. Folding the hero's two 3072 shared experts into one 6144 shared expert, which the summation makes equivalent, gives 13.25% with drops.

### Confidence

Medium-high on the numbers, lower on generality.

Run-to-run spread at fixed shape is about 0.7 points and tracks cluster load — the same configuration read 24.43% and 25.13% an hour apart. Every figure above with a single number is a single sample; the two that carry the argument have five and three repeats.

Correctness is gated at the hero widths on four GPUs: forward max absolute error 0.0625 against the ragged-a2a reference, every differentiable leaf within tolerance, relative L2 between 0.0044 and 0.0085 on all leaves, zero drops. Staged peer bytes halve exactly with the latent width, which is the expert-parallel traffic actually narrowing.

Two caveats:

- 48 layers at the hero routed width does not fit. The saved context needs a 163 GB allocation on device under `save_moe`, and the pinned-host allocator overflows under `offload_moe`. Cutting the routed macrobatch from 32,768 to 8,192 makes it fit and costs about 1.3 points. Activation memory sets this bound.
- These runs use eight experts at an expert axis of four. Per-token FLOPs are unchanged by expert count at top-4 routing, so MFU and tokens/s carry over, but 192 experts do not fit: expert weights shard only on the expert axis, so 192 over four ranks is 48 local experts and the optimizer state OOMs. Sharding them needs EP64.

### A gate shape that hid a deadlock

The first training run after the token-width split spun forever with every GPU at 100%.

`expert_grouped_gemm_kernel`'s non-wgrad path derives a barrier's required arrival count from `a_gmem.cols()`, which is already the routed width for routed tasks. The wgrad path cannot, because wgrad iterates K over token rows and `a_gmem.cols()` is the intermediate dim, so it takes the width as a parameter — and all three routed wgrads were handed the shared width. The waiter then demands `ceil(hidden/DISPATCH_Nb)` arrivals where only `ceil(routed/DISPATCH_Nb)` are ever published. `num_dispatch_tasks_of` and `num_combine_tasks_of` read the same shared width.

`DISPATCH_Nb` is 512. At the parity shape, hidden 512 against latent 256, both round to one block and agree by accident. At 6144 against 3072 it is a factor of two and the rank waits on a count that can never arrive.

Five sites moved to the routed width. A CPU test now pins the patched result — `d_y_shared.cols()` may appear in the generated backward only in the two definitions of the shared column-block count — so this cannot regress on a gate shape that happens not to expose it. The GPU gate runs the hero widths and hidden 1024 against latent 512, the smallest shape that straddles `DISPATCH_Nb`.

A compression ratio that divides evenly into a tile constant makes a whole class of width errors invisible. Gate shapes need to straddle `MLP_Nb` (256), `DISPATCH_Nb` (512), and `COMBINE_Nb`. Small and unequal is not sufficient. The intermediate split added the same class of site again in the two `*_row_block_ready_required_count` values, which count SwiGLU tiles across a path's intermediate width; each now has a per-side value.

### The fabric deadlock is independent of this work

Two 2-node `fabric_symmetric` runs identical but for `--latent-dim 3072` against `--latent-dim 0` both hang, so the cross-process deadlock is not caused by the two-width path. The same shape on one node under `in_process_peer` trains twenty of twenty updates.

It is more likely than the 29%-at-four-processes figure recorded earlier: seven of seven attempts at eight processes hung against a busy cluster. Neither `--mok-like-workspace-slots 2` nor the capacity-limited preset changes it. `MOK_TRACE_INVOCATIONS` shows every rank entering the same handler at the same generation and stopping inside it, which rules out a rank that failed to arrive and puts the fault in the backward comms with the full group present.

This gates `mok_like_num_devices` above four, which is what an EP64 expert axis needs. An expert axis of four keeps peers process-local and scales the rack by data parallelism, which is what the runs above use.

### Next

- Restore the wide routed macrobatch at 48 layers, which is the remaining throughput lever. Activation memory is what blocks it.
- 192 experts stays blocked behind EP64 and therefore behind the fabric deadlock.
- Nothing here is committed yet.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-17 — The hero moved to 8-of-384; every measurement branch is on the old shape

### Every measurement branch predates the current hero

`origin/main` changed `HERO_MODEL` in #8289 and #8348. Anything measured against a branch cut before
2026-08-16 22:42 UTC is a different model:

| `HERO_MODEL` on | routed experts | top-k | routed intermediate | shared intermediate | capacity factor | `moe_implementation` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `origin/main` | 384 | 8 | 3072 | 3072 | 1.15 | `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` |
| `mok-fabric-ep64` | 192 | 4 | 6144 | 3072 | 1.33 | `fixed_all_to_all` |
| `marin-ep-8081` | 192 | 4 | 6272 | 3072 | 1.33 | `fixed_all_to_all` |
| `research/mcwitt/8077-ragged-ep` | 192 | 4 | 6272 | 3072 | 1.33 | `fixed_all_to_all` |

Launcher flavors override `moe_implementation` per run, so the last column is the branch default
rather than what any given arm executed. The width and routing columns are not overridden.

Two consequences worth acting on.

Per-token cost at main's hero is 49.91 GFLOP against 47.4 for the old one, so tokens/s figures do
not transfer between them even at identical MFU. On sixty-four GB200s, 25% MFU is 267,000 tokens/s
at the new shape.

The routed and shared intermediates are equal on main. Any work whose motivation was the hero's
asymmetric intermediate widths — including the intermediate-width split in this branch — is no
longer load-bearing for the current architecture. The token-width asymmetry that `latent_dim`
drives still is.

### Top-8 was never gated

`TOP_K` was a module constant of 4 in `mok_like_correctness.py`. Every run of that harness,
including the ones behind the sealed v12 and v15 numbers, validated top-4 only; the hero has routed
top-8 since #8289. It is now a `--top-k` flag, and the fused kernel passes at the hero widths:

| quantity | value |
| --- | --- |
| forward max absolute error | 0.125 against peak magnitude 13.25 |
| forward relative L2 | 0.0062 |
| mismatch fraction | 0 |
| gradients within tolerance | 11 of 11, including `routed_x` and `latent_up` |
| dropped assignments | 0 |
| FFI calls per rank | one forward, one backward |

The call counts are load-bearing. One forward per rank confirms the combine is still named before
`latent_up` expands it; without that name the VJP recomputes the whole fused call and the forward
runs twice per layer, which shows up as halved throughput and no error at all.

The gate's bank is eight experts at top-8, so every token reaches every expert. That is a denser
capacity case than 8-of-384, not a weaker one. It does not cover the fabric transport, which is
single-process there.

### The EP64 OOM had already been solved on the ragged arm

The first 8-of-384 rack attempts died on the first `jit_train_step`, every rank at once:

```
ncclCuMemAlloc ... Cuda failure 2 'out of memory'
INTERNAL: NCCL operation ncclAlltoAll(send_contiguous, recv_contiguous, ...) failed
```

RA2A-002 hit this exact signature at EP64 and RA2A-003 cleared it: NCCL send/recv allocates a
dedicated FIFO per source-destination pair, so at sixty-three peers per rank the 4 MiB default
reserves about 252 MiB, and `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=1048576` brings that to about 63 MiB. That arm also
measured restoring 4 MiB as neutral wherever it already worked, so the change costs nothing.

Two more from MEP-032 are now carried as well: `--xla_gpu_enable_allocator_spatial_partitioning=false`,
because one shared pool otherwise reserves the whole of NCCL's window VA, and
`--xla_gpu_enable_dynamic_slice_fusion=false`, because the pass hides mosaic calls from XLA's
collective-buffer analysis.

Reading the arena arithmetic alongside those: the symmetric workspace is
`4 * tokens_per_rank * routed_dim * (1 + top_k)`, which at one rack is 7.50 GiB at top-4 and 13.50
GiB at top-8, and would be 27 GiB without the latent projection. It follows tokens per rank rather
than the routed macrobatch, so trading macrobatch away does not relieve it.

### A proxy that matched the wrong quantity

A two-node EP8 stand-in was submitted while the rack was gated, on the reasoning that tokens per
rank is 131,072 either way and therefore the arena is identical. That holds for the arena and fails
for everything else: expert weights and optimizer state shard on the expert axis, so 384 experts
over eight ranks is forty-eight local experts against the rack's six. It died on a single 145.3 GB
allocation, a shape that does not exist at EP64.

Wider expert parallelism makes this configuration easier rather than harder, which is why the
substitution looked safe. Proxies for this model are only valid for quantities that follow tokens
per rank.

### Status

No 8-of-384 EP64 throughput number yet. The rack job is Kueue-gated behind production capacity, and
the three attempts before it failed on the OOM above, which is now addressed but unverified at
sixty-four ranks.

Retracted from earlier comments on this issue: the claim that the goal's MFU and tokens/s targets
were mutually inconsistent. That was derived from this branch's stale 6144 routed intermediate. At
main's hero the two figures are the same bar.

🤖

## 2026-08-17 — Main's hero runs dropless at 25.3% MFU at node scale; two EP64 hypotheses killed

### The shape works

`mok-hero384-ep4-16l-20260816`: one node, EP4, main's hero shape — hidden 6144, latent 3072, routed
and shared intermediate 3072, top-8, two shared experts — sixteen layers, batch 128 per node so
tokens per rank is 131,072 and the arena matches a rack's 13.50 GiB. Thirty-two experts, eight local
per rank.

| steps 11-24 | value |
| --- | --- |
| MFU | 25.08% low, 25.56% high |
| tokens/s on four GPUs | 47,419 - 48,355 |
| drop fraction | zero from step 19 |

Expert count does not enter per-token FLOPs at fixed top-k and MFU is depth-neutral at fixed
macrobatch, so this should carry to 384 experts and forty-eight layers. It does not carry to EP64,
for two reasons worth stating: the run shards non-expert parameters over four devices where a rack
shards over sixty-four, and it uses a forward path that a cross-process transport cannot.

Doubling active experts from top-4 to top-8 did not cost MFU. That is the load-bearing claim for the
8/384 architecture and it now has a measurement behind it.

### Staging does not explain the EP64 deficit

`MokLikeConfig` rejects both direct-read peer modes when the transport crosses processes, so EP64
must run `forward_x_storage=RUNTIME_STAGED` while the run above used `XLA_PEER_EXPERIMENTAL` with
zero forward staging. That looked like the EP64 tax. It is not.

| forward storage | forward staging bytes | MFU, steps 17-24 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `XLA_PEER_EXPERIMENTAL` | 0 | 25.08 - 25.56% |
| `RUNTIME_STAGED` | 1.29 TB | 25.17 - 25.68% |

One field changed, everything else held. The staging happened and cost nothing measurable; the
forced arm is marginally faster, which is noise. The copy is arena-local HBM traffic at both widths
and cheap against the expert GEMMs.

This kills a change before anyone writes it. The obvious remedy — mapping XLA buffers into the
fabric so the forward keeps its in-place read at EP64 — would be substantial kernel and runtime work
against a cost that measures as zero.

### Peer-wait counters are not a time proxy

`mok_like/runtime/*/peer_wait_cycles_total` looked like a cost attribution: `backward_pre` carries
73.9% of all peer waiting across 1.7 million events. In the A/B above that same counter rose 24%,
from 229.6 to 284.3 billion cycles, and MFU did not move outside the noise band.

The counters record how long warps sit on arrival flags. Overlapped waiting and exposed waiting look
identical in them. They are useful for finding a hang and misleading for attributing time; pair them
with a profile before drawing a conclusion, which is what I failed to do.

### Also

The event simulator in `experiments/marin_ep/perfmodel/eventsim.py` predicts the fused transport is
essentially invariant to expert-axis width at main's hero widths: +1.3% from EP4 to EP64 under
balanced routing and -0.1% with one expert at four times the mean, against +10.6% and +14.2% for a
bulk-synchronous shape. Consistent with the staging result — the wire is not what grows. Treat as a
hypothesis generator: it models the `marin_ep` transport rather than the megakernel, excludes SM
contention between transport and MMA warps by its own fidelity notes, and its API changed under me
mid-experiment, so the numbers come from a moving snapshot rather than a pinned commit.

No EP64 throughput number yet. That job has been Kueue-gated for four hours behind seven rack-scale
jobs, and the fabric transport hung again at eight processes carrying all three of the borrowed
NCCL and XLA workarounds, which is what their mechanisms predict since none of them touch the
megakernel's own transport.

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 
## MoK at rack scale: what runs, and why the next step is removing `fabric_symmetric`

Status update from EP64 bringup. **No performance result yet** — this is a working test surface plus a scoped recommendation on the transport, backed by a clean same-day differential that isolates the failure to one component.

### 1. What now runs

| arm | transport | scale | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mok_like` (in-repo kernel) | `fabric_symmetric` | EP16 (4 nodes) | **25/25 steps** |
| `mok_like` (in-repo kernel) | `fabric_symmetric` | EP32 (8 nodes) | **25/25 steps** |
| `mok_like` (in-repo kernel) | `fabric_symmetric` | EP64 (16 nodes) | **wedges** — 4 attempts, best = 1 step |
| upstream `mok` wheel | Torch symmetric memory | EP64 (16 nodes) | **25/25 steps** |
| `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` | — | EP64 (16 nodes) | 25/25 steps |

All arms: hero 8-of-384, 16 layers, 25 steps, GB200, `cw-us-east-08a`, one rack for the EP64 rows.

Of the four `fabric_symmetric` EP64 attempts, three reached the kernel and wedged; one died in preflight on an unrelated packaging bug that is now fixed (§4).

**No cross-row performance claim is made or implied.** Global batch scales with node count, so the EP16/EP32 rows do a quarter and a half of the EP64 work per step. The upstream-wheel row is a different model configuration as well — see §3 — so it is not a MoK-vs-pooled-wave datapoint either. The matched comparison does not exist yet, because the in-repo kernel does not run at EP64.

### 2. The EP64 failure on `fabric_symmetric`

**Signature.** All 64 ranks report every MoK generation for the step, then permanent silence. Python stacks (via SIGTERM) show every rank blocked inside the compiled executable at `train_step`. No exception, no NaN, `failures=0`, tasks still `running`. It never self-terminates: `WaitCompletionKernel` spins on `__nanosleep(64)` checking only for cancellation, with no deadline, so one wedge held a rack for an hour before it was killed by hand. (`kWorkspaceAcquireTimeout` already guards workspace acquisition at 5 minutes — the completion wait never got the equivalent.)

**Not an integer-width bug.** `RankMask` is `uint64_t`, and `kAllRanksMask` correctly special-cases 64 to `~0` rather than the undefined `1 << 64`. Debug-counter storage derives from `kPeerWaitCellCount = 4 * kNumDevices` with static asserts, so there is no out-of-bounds write at 64 either.

**Not the stock-PJRT peer cap.** `MultiGpuBarrierWithNcclKernel`'s `kMaxPeers=32` (#8313, openxla/xla#47283) was the leading suspect. Two independent results retire it. The wedge reproduces with the kmax128 patched wheel confirmed loaded (`pjrt 0.11.1.dev0+selfbuilt`); and separately, a 64-rank run completed 25/25 steps of FSDP and XLA collectives on **stock** PJRT (§3), so the cap does not block 64-rank collectives in general.

**Not the rack placement.** A 16-node GB200 gang is hard-bound to a single NVLink domain by the scheduler: `gpu_gang_coscheduling_level()` returns `COSCHEDULE_NVLINK_DOMAIN` for `replicas <= SCHEDULABLE_RACK_NODES` (16), which maps to a required topology constraint. CoreWeave keeps 16 of each rack's 18 nodes schedulable, so 16 is deliberately the largest gang that can be hard-bound to one domain, and `HERO_EP_NODES = 16` sits on that boundary by design. The `fabric_workspace.cuh` comment reasoning about "16 nodes x 4 GPUs = 64 GPUs" is correct, and single-domain placement is guaranteed rather than assumed.

**A unique JAX coordinator port helps but does not fix it.** Submitting with a per-gang `IRIS_PORT_JAX` advanced the wedge from step 1 to step 2 and produced the first completed step from any `fabric_symmetric` EP64 run.

**Which peer fails to arrive is still unknown**, because a wedge currently names nothing — see the last paragraph of §3.

### 3. Why the next step is removing `fabric_symmetric`

`fabric_symmetric` — a Marin-owned CUDA VMM workspace with exported fabric handles — is today the *only* cross-node transport for the in-repo kernel. `in_process_peer` publishes peer pointers through a process-local registry, so it caps an expert group at one node's four GPUs. EP64 therefore rests entirely on the fabric path, and that path has never completed an EP64 run.

**A same-day differential isolates the transport.** The upstream prebuilt `mok` wheel, driven over `torch.distributed._symmetric_memory` on a plain NCCL process group, completed **25/25 steps at 64 ranks on one rack**, first attempt, no tuning, on stock PJRT (`jax[cuda13]==0.11.0`, no patched wheel), with `moe/drop_fraction` 0 at every step. Same cluster, same rack size, same 64 ranks, same hard single-domain placement, same routed shape the fabric arm wedges on (E384, top-8, 6 local experts per rank, hidden 6144, 16 layers, seq 4096) — run within the same hour.

The one hero parameter that arm cannot express is `latent_dim`, which postdates that code path, so its routed experts are 6144→3072→6144 instead of 3072→3072→3072 — **twice the routed width, i.e. a harder arm, not an easier one.** That is also why its throughput is not comparable to the pooled-wave row and is omitted here.

So the variable is neither EP64, nor the rack, nor 64-rank collectives, nor the cluster, nor the model shape, nor stock-vs-patched PJRT. It is the fabric transport specifically.

**What the swap was meant to buy, and what it actually buys.** `fabric_symmetric` replaced a rendezvous built on PyTorch's `_symmetric_memory` with one Marin owns outright. The upside is real but narrow: no dependency on a private Torch API, exact control of mapping, alignment, access flags and lifetime, and the runtime packaged as a single native extension. What it does not buy is the thing that would justify the cost — the workspace is not allocated by XLA in either design, so it stays invisible to XLA's allocator whichever rendezvous is underneath. Both designs are fabric/IMEX rendezvous underneath; the change moves *who owns the memory*, not *what the kernel does*, so there is no throughput gain to expect from it.

**The cost has landed on the hard half.** Owning the transport means owning fabric export-import, address reservation and mapping, peer-pointer exchange, teardown, rollback, and attempt-scoped rendezvous — and getting all of it right at 64 ranks across 16 hosts. That is exactly where we are stuck, and the same kernel and ABI run clean at 16 and 32 ranks.

**Proposal.** Stop treating `fabric_symmetric` as the EP64 path. Keep `MokLikeWorkspaceTransport` pluggable and restore the Torch rendezvous as the supported cross-process transport, so EP64 work proceeds on a layer with a demonstrated 64-rank result at hero shape while the kernel work continues. Revisit a Marin-owned VMM workspace when there is a measured reason — Torch API instability, teardown, or an allocator-budget conflict — rather than on general principle.

One caveat worth recording: a standalone 64-rank symmetric-memory probe on the same day did *not* fail to establish, but did abort at the first device barrier, with all 63 other ranks naming rank 23 as the peer that never signalled within the 180 s timeout. A single-rank straggler is a different failure class from a rendezvous that cannot form — and the full training run through the same layer succeeded — but the Torch path is not being claimed as flawless.

Two things make the swap cheap. Running both transports against the same kernel and ABI is also the cleanest way to localise the fabric defect, with no device-side instrumentation. And whichever way it goes, `WaitCompletionKernel` should get a deadline plus a diagnostic naming the peers whose completion stamp never landed — today a wedge is indistinguishable from slowness and holds hardware until a human intervenes. The Torch layer already produces exactly that diagnostic, which is how the straggler above was identified in seconds.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The EP64 wedge on `fabric_symmetric` was an uninitialized arena. It is fixed, and the transport now completes EP64 at hero shape.

**Root cause.** `CreateLocalSegment` (`csrc/fabric_workspace.cuh`) allocates the symmetric arena with `cuMemCreate` and never zeroed it. The arena holds `generation`, `forward/backward_input_ready`, `forward/backward_completions`, and `cancellation`. The `cudaMalloc` path in `mok_forward_ffi.cu` memsets all seven at startup; the arena path memset only `debug_counters` and `last_forward_completion`, which are not arena-backed. `cuMemCreate` does not guarantee zeroed pages.

The device protocol compares monotonically, and the first generation stamped is `(1 << 1) | slot` = 2. Any flag word arriving >= 2 is indistinguishable from a peer that already completed or already failed. A rank that reads its own `cancellation` as set returns without stamping, and every peer then spins in the untimed `WaitCompletionKernel` loop.

**Fix.** `cuMemsetD8` plus `cuCtxSynchronize` in `CreateLocalSegment`, before the handle is exported. The memset precedes the host-side `process_allgather`, which is a barrier, so no peer can import the arena until every rank has zeroed.

**Evidence.**

| arm | transport | scale | layers | latent_dim | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mok_like` | `fabric_symmetric` | EP64 (16 nodes) | 48 | 3072 | 200/200 steps, 21.28% MFU, loss 10.7 -> 3.32 |
| `mok_like` | `fabric_symmetric` | EP4 (1 tray, 4 processes) | 4 | 3072 | 5 of 5 runs completed; previously wedged ~29% |

Run `goal-ep64-48l-run3` on `cw-us-east-08a`: 8-of-384 top-8, two shared experts, d6144, 32768 tokens per rank (one kernel macrobatch), peak 157.4 GiB per rank.

The rank-count pattern reported above (EP16 and EP32 clean, EP64 wedging 4 of 4) follows from this mechanism: more nodes means more chances that one arena arrives dirty.

**Why earlier attempts on this file showed nothing.** `fabric_workspace.cuh` was not in the native build cache key. `_build_path` hashed `mok_forward_ffi.cu` and the patched upstream tree only, so editing that header left the digest unchanged and relinked the cached `libmok_forward_ffi.so` without running nvcc. Any earlier conclusion that a change to this header had no effect was measured on an unchanged binary. The key now covers `csrc/*.cuh`.

**Limits of this result.** One EP64 run plus five one-tray runs. The arena is zeroed once at init, so the trial count is process startups, not kernel invocations.

The recommendation to give `WaitCompletionKernel` a deadline and a diagnostic naming the peers whose stamp never landed stands independently of transport choice.

Two further traps on this path:

- The megakernel nvcc build for a new `num_devices` runs lazily inside the first FFI call, so a fresh node sits in `pxla.py:420` for 15-25 minutes building the kernel. That is compilation, not a wedge. Two healthy rack runs were killed here before it was recognized.
- `Can't reduce memory use below N by rematerialization` is an intermediate-pass message, not the final allocation. Probes emitting it at 240 GiB report a 157 GiB peak and then succeed.

comments.body:
🤖 Correction to my earlier comment in this thread. Two claims there are wrong, and the fix is weaker than I stated.

**1. The megakernel build is fast; long silences are wedges, not compilation.**

I attributed 15-25 minute silences at `pxla.py:420` to a lazy nvcc build inside the first FFI call. That is wrong. With `_BUILD_SCHEMA` bumped to force a full rebuild, a 16-node EP64 job reached training step 4 in **196 seconds** from submission, including the kernel build, JAX init, model init and XLA compile. Any silence of more than a few minutes past the rematerialization warnings is a wedge. Two runs I described as killed mid-compile were wedged.

**2. Zeroing the arena is necessary but not sufficient at EP64.**

The fix stands on its own evidence: one-tray EP4 went 0/5 wedges against a ~29% prior rate, and it produced the first 200-step EP64 run at hero shape (21.28% MFU, loss 10.7 -> 3.32). But EP64 keeps wedging.

| run | delta from baseline | outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `goal-ep64-48l-run3` | none | 200/200 steps |
| `basewedge-a` | none, rebuild forced | 25/25 steps, 21.24% MFU |
| `goal-ep64-48l-b32` | device fraction 0.88 | ~18 min silent, wedged |
| `mfu-comm56` | `num_comm_sms` 56/40 | ~33 min silent, wedged |
| `mfu-comm24` | `num_comm_sms` 24/16 | ~31 min silent, wedged |
| `mfu-cf10` | capacity factor 1.0 | ~43 min silent, wedged |

Baseline is 2 of 3; every non-baseline configuration wedged. So a second defect remains that arena initialization does not cover. Separately, `num_comm_sms` is not a free knob: 56/40 and 24/16 both wedge while the tuned 40/28 runs, which points at a coupling between comm CTA count and internal partitioning.

**3. The peer-wait deadline is implemented, and it did not fire.**

About 200 s in both `WaitCompletionKernel` and the generated `system_generation_wait`; on expiry it prints the waiting rank, the peer, the target generation and the observed value, then stamps cancellation. `mfu-cf10` wedged for 43 minutes with this compiled in and produced no diagnostic.

That is itself a result. `WaitCompletionKernel` is launched after the megakernel, so a hang inside the megakernel's own `gpu`-scope barriers never reaches it, and a device `printf` from a kernel that never exits cannot flush. The remaining wedge is therefore most likely inside the megakernel's internal barriers rather than the cross-rank generation protocol. Bounding those is the next diagnostic step, and it needs to be done inside the kernel where the barrier waits live.

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 **MoK now matches pooled-wave at hero shape.** EP64, 100 steps, one rack per arm, submitted 8 s apart.

| steps 90–99 (converged) | MoK | pooled-wave |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tokens/s | **237,613** | 237,310 |
| step time | 17.653 s | 17.675 s |
| analytic MFU | 22.24% | 22.21% |
| `moe/drop_fraction` | 0.00000 (all 100 steps) | 0.0072 |

MoK is ahead by 0.13% — 0.023 ± 0.061 s, t = 0.37. **Read this as a tie**, not a win: it is an order of magnitude inside the ~0.6–1% rack-to-rack variability, and the two arms were on different racks (a 16-node gang binds to one NVLink domain; an NVL72 rack holds 18).

### What changed

The fused call now owns the entire MoE. Previously the JAX side computed the LatentMoE projections itself and handed the kernel a zeroed 256-wide dummy shared expert; now `W_down`, the RMSNorm, `W_up`, and both real shared experts all live inside one megakernel launch.

The blocker was never the kernel — it was width. Under LatentMoE the routed path carries `latent_dim`-wide rows (3072) while the shared path stays at hidden (6144). The megakernel already handled two widths internally; the host wrappers and the XLA FFI adapter both assumed one. Splitting them is what made the hero shape expressible at all.

One thing worth flagging for anyone touching that code: width confusion here is invisible to tests. Splitting the widths introduced a deadlock in which seven sites in the *backward* sized routed work from the shared width, so the routed weight-gradients waited on `ceil(H/DISPATCH_Nb)` dispatch arrivals when only `ceil(L/DISPATCH_Nb)` are ever produced. Every suite passed, because every suite ran H == L.

### Why the earlier 25-step number was misleading

A 25-step version of this comparison put pooled-wave ahead by 3.48%. That was an artifact of run length.

- **pooled-wave is converged by step 2** and then drifts *upward* — +0.008 s/step over steps 50–99, t = 7.16 — tracking its falling drop fraction, since fewer drops mean more routed tokens actually reach an expert.
- **MoK ramps for ~85 steps.** Step time falls monotonically from 48 s to 17.65 s; the slope is −0.030 s/step over 50–99 (t = −13.1) and only becomes statistically indistinguishable from zero at about step 85.

At step 24 you catch MoK mid-descent. Anyone benchmarking a dropless backend against an untrained router should budget ≥100 steps.

### Drops do not need discounting

The natural correction — scale the baseline down by its drop fraction — is wrong, and it is worth knowing why. `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` sizes receiver buffers from `capacity_factor` at trace time and runs a dense GEMM over every slot, filled or not. At hero shape that is `ceil(1.15 × 524,288 / 18) = 33,497` rows per expert-wave, `3 × 6 × 33,497 = 602,946` rows executed against 524,288 analytic — exactly 1.15×, independent of how much it drops. **A capacity drop discards useful output, not work**, so the wall-clock correction is exactly zero.

If you want goodput rather than throughput, the discount is `drop × routed_flops_fraction` = 0.0072 × 0.4356 = 0.31%, giving MoK +0.44% instead of +0.13%. Still a tie. (The same fixed-capacity behaviour also means the baseline's *utilization* MFU is understated by ~6.5%, so the two MFU columns are biased in opposite directions and only the tokens/s ranking is safe to read directly.)

### Scope

Both arms ran the full 359.6B hero: 384 routed experts, top-8, 48 layers, seq 4096, batch 1024, hidden 6144, latent 3072, capacity 1.15, transport 1.15, 3 waves. The resolved configs differ in **10 keys of 234** — the backend selection, five keys strictly downstream of it, the wheel pin, and run identity.

Two deviations to record. Both arms ran four processes per node, which MoK requires for Torch symmetric memory, rather than the hero's native one per node; #8209 measured that difference at this exact shape as −0.22%, inside the ±0.25% floor, with identical peak HBM. And MoK ran with contiguous expert placement — the `r9_profile_hot_cold` treatment is gated to 128 experts and is structurally inapplicable at 384, where each rank holds six experts rather than a hot/cold pair.

### Where the code is

Marin side: branch [`mark/mok-wheel-latent`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/mark/mok-wheel-latent). Jobs `mhep-{mok-latent,pooled-wave}-ep64-100s-20260819`.

Kernel side: [`muchanem/mixture-of-kittens`](https://github.com/muchanem/mixture-of-kittens/tree/mark/mok_hacking), branch `mark/mok_hacking` — a fork of [`cursor/mixture-of-kittens`](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens), which carries none of this. It is pinned as a submodule at `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/mixture-of-kittens` (the repo's first, so nothing implies `--recurse-submodules`):

```
git submodule update --init experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/mixture-of-kittens
```

The fork's history is the readable account, in dependency order: separate token widths for the routed and shared paths, a routed-only epilogue, the LatentMoE projections as fused kernels in `csrc/latent.cuh`, and `csrc/ffi_adapter.cuh` — the only surface Marin calls — widened to carry both. The in-tree wheel is built from the pinned commit; the training arm installs it directly rather than building at job time.

Given the delta is well under the two-rack confound, the way to tighten it is a rerun with the arms swapped between racks, or sequentially on one.

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 Profiling report:

## Jobs and terminal states

| run | state |
|---|---|
| XProf pass — [MoK](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhprof-mok-hero-xprof-r1-20260819), [pooled-wave](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhprof-wave-hero-xprof-r1-20260819) | **succeeded**, 16/16, exit 0, 0 preemptions, 1 h 07 m 56 s |
| Nsight pass — [MoK](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhprofn-mok-hero-nsys-r2-20260819), [pooled-wave](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhprofn-wave-hero-nsys-r2-20260819) | **succeeded**, 16/16, exit 0 |
| Nsight export/reduction (CPU only, no W&B run) | **succeeded**, 1/1, 1 m 43 s |

**Both instruments captured successfully.** All 128 XPlanes (64 ranks × 2 arms) carry an active `/device:GPU:0` plane; kernel-event counts are identical on every rank (MoK 294,580, pooled-wave 365,190), exactly 5 consecutive `jit_train_step` executes per rank, uploaded to `steps-90-to-95`. Nsight's CUPTI kernel counts match XProf's *exactly*, from a different instrument on a different rack.

Raw captures are on CoreWeave S3 in `marin-us-east-02a` (endpoint `https://cwobject.com`, virtual-hosted addressing):

```text
tmp/ttl=30d/xprof/mhprof-mok-hero-xprof-r1-20260819/    128 objects,  8,497,162,583 B
tmp/ttl=30d/xprof/mhprof-wave-hero-xprof-r1-20260819/   128 objects, 10,333,899,549 B
  -> process-000NN/plugins/profile/steps-90-to-95/{*.xplane.pb,*.trace.json.gz}, 64 ranks per arm

tmp/ttl=30d/iris-profiles/k3sc0re/mok-vs-pooled-wave-hero-20260819/   22 objects, 258,107,340 B
  -> mok/r00000-s1zsxs64.nsys-rep, wave/r00000-s1zsxs64.nsys-rep
  -> analysis/r1/  (nsys stats CSVs, gzipped SQLite exports, custom reductions, report SHA-256s)
```

**The bucket lifecycle expires them around 2026-09-18.**

## Top findings

**1. The tie does not reproduce on one rack.** Two independent single-rack replicates, unprofiled steps 85-89: MoK −1.586% (t=−2.90) and −0.498% (t=−2.46). Both negative, both significant, disagreeing by 1.1 points — which is itself the rack-to-rack effect. The head-to-head's +0.128% was a two-rack artifact.

**2. MoK is not losing on FLOPs, and its dropless advantage is far smaller than the 1.15× capacity factor suggests.** Measured from the HLO: the baseline's routed GEMMs run at literally `bf16[6,33497,3072]`, i.e. 602,946 rows vs 524,288 assignments (1.14835×). But that lands on the routed term, which is 43.56% of analytic FLOPs → **1.065× on the whole step, not 1.15×**. And MoK gives it back: its backward replays 49 of 65 minibatches (`num_minibatches - num_minibatches_of(0)`), worth 7.41% of the analytic step. Net executed routed-expert FLOPs: baseline 6.555e15/step vs MoK 6.436e15 — **1.9% apart**, and within 0.4% on the whole step. (My predicted 6.555e15 matched the measured value exactly; the shared-expert term cross-checked to four digits.)

**3. MoK is losing on concurrency.** MoK's MoE path is **1.47 s/step cheaper** in summed kernel time (10.065 vs 11.531 s) and still ends up 0.38 s/step behind, because the baseline hides **2.21 s/step more** work: concurrency surplus 2.559 vs 0.348 s/step, with `SendRecv` 64% overlapped by GEMMs. Nsight independently gives 2.556 vs 0.354.

**4. The barrier is 99.8% skew, but the skew is mostly hardware.** Per-instance minimum wait across ranks sums to 0.0020 s/step against a 1.030 s/step mean — so it is skew, not uniform exposed comm. But the pooled-wave control, whose per-rank work is provably identical, shows the *same* 7-31% cross-rank time spread, absorbed in `SendRecv` at corr −0.9894. Per-launch max/mean is 1.089/1.133 raw against a hardware-only null of **1.065**.

**5. Comm SM reservation is 26.3% of the chip (forward).** 40 and 28 CTAs of `smCount` 152, at 232 KB shared → exactly one CTA/SM, so those are whole SMs held for the kernel's lifetime. Achieved: forward 1,239 TFLOP/s (67.3% of what its 112 SMs can do), backward 1,064 (52.2% of 124 SMs); the baseline's routed cuBLAS GEMMs do 1,537 TFLOP/s on all 152.

## Rank-level imbalance and the placement ceiling

- **max/mean per barrier**: fwd p50 1.0896, bwd p50 1.1327 raw; 1.0674 / 1.1064 with per-GPU speed removed; null 1.0646.
- **persistent vs transient**: rank + rank×layer = 31.0% (fwd) / 34.2% (bwd) of the variance; **rank×layer×step transient = 68.6% / 65.6%**.
- **ceiling**: oracle static per-layer placement recovers **0.338 s/step = 1.94%**, against 2.21 s/step for overlap and 0.68 s/step for the replay. Placement is the smallest lever.
- **pooled-wave control**: per-rank work constant (identical kernel counts and compile-time shapes), but per-rank *time* varies 8-16% — same as MoK. This is the reason MoK's barrier asymmetry must not be read as routing skew.
- **QB (quantile balancing)**: confirmed active, and bit-identical on both arms — `loss = cross_entropy_loss` only (`model.py:1452`), `z_loss_weight` is the final-logit logsumexp term, and QB is `router_bias = -qb_beta` under `stop_gradient` feeding top-(K+1). Both arms bit-identical.

## Not collected, and why

- **Peak HBM.** Neither instrument sampled device memory, and `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` bypasses the BFC allocator xprof instruments. I have peak pinned *host* memory (79.20 GB of a 206.16 GB arena) and MoK's declared FFI buffers from the HLO (backward scratch `u8[6871631872]` = 6.87 GB) instead.
- **Tensor-core utilisation.** `is_kernel_using_tensor_core` is `false` for every kernel in both arms including the cuBLAS GEMMs, and `mxu_utilization_percent` is 0.0% — the detectors do not work for SM100 in this xprof build. I substituted achieved FLOP/s from HLO shapes and measured durations.
- **Launch-space overhead cost.** The grid is 32× oversized (114,068 useful clusters of 2,906,132 launched) but is byte-identical on all 720 launches, so the traces cannot price it. Named as an A/B, not costed.

## Measured vs inferred

**Measured**: all kernel times, counts, grids, occupancy, overlap, per-rank spreads, HLO shapes and the baseline's executed FLOPs, `smCount` 152, throughput, memcpy bytes. **Inferred**: MoK's routed row count (524,288 + 256-row padding — dropless semantics plus source, not observable in the trace), hence its replay count (49/65) and its megakernel FLOPs; and the split of the backward megakernel into dgrad+wgrad+replay, which is forced by arithmetic but not separable inside a fused kernel.

spillover_issues.author: muchanem
spillover_issues.body:
An Iris CPU request carries no placement constraint at all: fray's `CpuConfig`
maps to `device=None`, so a CPU-only task cannot say which scale group or CPU
architecture it needs. Selecting pools would allow fine-grained selection of
CPU architecture — workloads that depend on ISA features (for example x86
AMX/VNNI INT8 paths that OpenVINO's ARM plugin does not take) have no way to
require them, and on mixed x86/aarch64 clusters such as `cw-us-east-08a` the
placement outcome just follows whichever pool has warm nodes.

The wire path is closer to done than it looks. `pool` is already a recognized
placement key in the k8s backend (`_CONSTRAINT_KEY_TO_NODE_LABEL` in
`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py`) and constraints already
reach the pod builder — but no node carries the `iris.pool` label the key
resolves to, so a `pool` constraint today pends forever. The Kueue CPU flavor
on 08a is selector-less, and Iris itself does not place tasks on this backend;
Kueue owns placement.

`.agents/projects/2026-07-30_iris_pool_arch_selection.md` (landing on main in #7860) works through the
details and proposes a fix in two complementary parts, neither touching a
proto:

1. Derive the constraint→node-label map from the cluster's `label_prefix` so
   `pool` resolves to the scale-group label nodes actually carry, re-add
   `ResourceConfig.pool` in fray (re-applying the `20b7003fe` removal), and add
   `arch` → `kubernetes.io/arch`. `arch` is the highest-value line in the
   change: it states "must run on x86" without naming a pool or hard-coding
   cluster topology.
2. Pin the Kueue CPU resource flavor on 08a to `cpu-erapids` so CPU-only pods
   default to x86 with no client change. A safe cluster-global default, not a
   substitute for (1).

Estimated surface is ~5 source files, ~40 lines. The project note also records
the landmines — `iris.region` hard-fails on non-EQ operators in the same code
path, only EQ is supported for `nodeSelector`, the controller must be
redeployed, the Kueue change is a Pulumi apply with a different blast radius,
and the autoscaler's constraint routing needs a check so an unadvertised
`pool` key cannot starve demand.

Verify before writing code: the claim that no node carries `iris.pool` is
static inference from `nodepool_manifests.py`. One
`kubectl get nodes --show-labels` on 08a should confirm it, and confirm
`kubernetes.io/arch` is present.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
Ran the "verify before writing code" checks on `cw-us-east-08a` (2026-08-13T21:01Z). All three static inferences hold:

**`iris.pool` is absent on every node** — confirmed. A `pool` constraint would pend forever today, as the issue predicts.

**`kubernetes.io/arch` is present** — the `gb200-4x` nodes are `arm64` and the `cd-gp-i64-erapids` nodes are `amd64`. The `arch` → `kubernetes.io/arch` mapping in part (1) works against real labels, and the x86/aarch64 split falls exactly along the CPU/GPU pool boundary.

**The scale-group label is scoped as described** — nodes carry `iris-cw-use08a-scale-group` ∈ {`gb200`, `cpu-erapids`}, not `iris.pool`. Deriving the map from `label_prefix` resolves against these.

---

One conflict worth folding into part (2) before it ships.

**Pinning the 08a Kueue CPU flavor to `cpu-erapids` would make current CPU production work unschedulable.** `rav.datakit-fuzzy-validation-current-focus-prod-v16` requests per pod roughly 80% of a GB200 node's allocatable CPU and 90% of its memory, and is running many such pods right now. A `cd-gp-i64-erapids` node has well under half the cores one of those pods asks for, so pinned to that pool the job would not fit on any node, at any replica count — and the pool as a whole is a small fraction of what the job currently consumes.

That sizing is not accidental: the request is shaped to nearly fill a GB200 node and is only satisfiable there. A cluster-global default that assumes accelerator-free work fits the CPU pool does not hold on 08a.

This is not an argument against part (2) — the safe-default intent is right, and part (1) is unaffected. But the default needs a fallback path (or an explicit opt-out) for accelerator-free pods too large for the pinned pool, otherwise the change converts today's GPU-stranding into a hard pend for a production job. Worth deciding which of those failure modes is preferred, explicitly.

For context on the stranding half: that job's placement currently holds a large set of GB200 nodes at zero GPUs used, putting most of the cluster's idle GPUs out of reach. Filed as #8247 — it's a placement/packing gap rather than a pool-selection one, but the two interact directly, since a working `pool`/`arch` selector plus adequate CPU capacity would be the cleanest fix for both.
